World.title: Is the peso punching above its weight? The results of our latest MND Peso Index™
World.content:
THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience

MND Intelligence · Fourth edition

Welcome to the fourth edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily.

The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued or undervalued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas.

Unlike previous editions, our latest MND Peso Index™ assessment is being published in the same month as its underlying price survey, making it even more timely.

Our headline finding for August 2026 indicates that the peso was overvalued against the dollar by 2.4%, a decrease of 0.5 percentage points compared to the 2.9% overvaluation we determined in late June.

For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May.

What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in August 2026?

In August 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, overvalued the Mexican peso by 2.4%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Aug. 6, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.64 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 17.22 pesos per dollar on Aug. 6.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 17.22 to the US dollar — was overvalued by 2.4% in early August.

In other words, the USD:MXN exchange rate — if it reflected the rate at which the peso could buy the basket’s goods and services in Mexico at the same dollar prices as in the United States — would be 17.64.

In the table below, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (ie., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the overvaluation assessment for the peso.

If the implied rate is lower than the current exchange rate, it implies that the item is less expensive in Mexico than you would expect it to be, and vice versa.

Why did the peso’s ‘overvalued’ assessment decrease between late June and August?

The MND Peso Rate — the mean implied exchange rate — changed considerably between late June and early August, declining by 37 centavos from 18.01 to 17.64.

The difference between the Banxico USD:MXN fix rate we used in late June (17.50) and that we used in early August (17.22) was 28 centavos. In an article published last Friday, we wrote about the reasons why the peso has recently appreciated.

The gap between the MND Peso Rate and Banxico’s FIX rate in early August was 42 centavos, down from 51 centavos in late June. The narrowing of the gap between the two rates is the reason why the peso’s overvaluation assessment fell from 2.9% in late June to 2.4% in early August.

But why, you might wonder, did the MND Peso Rate come down? The decline was the result of changes in the implied rates for seven of the 20 goods and services. The implied rates for the other 13 goods and services stayed the same between late June and early August.

The implied rates for four products — diapers, a hose, motor oil and eggs — declined. In the case of the diapers and the motor oil, the implied rate declined because prices in Mexico fell. In the case of the hose and the eggs, the implied rate declined because prices in Dallas increased.

The implied rates for two goods and one service — dog food, a Costco rotisserie chicken and pet grooming — increased. In the case of the dog food and the rotisserie chicken, the implied rates increased due to price increases in Mexico. In the case of the pet grooming, the implied rate increased due to a price reduction in Dallas.

Overall, the combined downward effect of the four lower implied rates outweighed the upward effect of the three higher rates. Thus the MND Peso Rate fell between late June and early August.

The cost of the Mexican and US baskets both fell in August

While the MND Peso Index™ is NOT a cost-of-living index, it is worth noting that the total costs of the Mexican and U.S. baskets of goods and services were lower in early August than in late June. However, the reduction was minimal in both cases.

The basket of goods and services in Mexico cost 5,650 pesos on Aug. 6, a reduction of 59 pesos, or 1%, compared to June 29. The slight decline in the cost of the Mexican basket in early August came at a time when inflation was easing, with Mexico’s annual headline rate falling to 3.12% in July from 3.37% in June.

The basket of goods and services in Dallas cost $350.68 on Aug. 6, a reduction of $3.50, or 1%, compared to June 29. The slight decline in the cost of the Dallas basket in early August came at a time when inflation in the United States was also slowing, with the annual headline rate in the U.S. falling to 3.4% in July from 3.5% in June.

Although the cost of the Mexican basket declined in peso terms between late June and early August, its price increased when converted to dollars because the peso appreciated 1.6% in the period. The cost of the Mexican basket rose to US $328.12 on Aug. 6 from $326.21 on June 29.

The MND Peso Index™ has now found the peso to be overvalued in April, May, June and August

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June and 2.4% in early August.

The difference between the lowest overvaluation assessment — our most recent one — and the highest is just 1.6 percentage points.

So far in 2026, the peso has appreciated 5.4% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Aug. 11 was 17.08. If the Banxico FIX rate was 17.08 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Aug. 6, the overvaluation assessment for the peso would have been 3.3%.

* Price sources: Mexico prices were collected from the websites and apps of Walmart México, Costco México, AutoZone México, Telmex, Cinépolis, Petco México, McDonald’s, Starbucks, Netflix, Spotify and Microsoft. Dallas prices were collected from their U.S. equivalents. The Banxico FIX rate of 17.22 published on Aug. 6, 2026, was used as the official exchange rate reference.

World.title: Sheinbaum celebrates Mexico’s historic medal haul at 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💰 All CAC Games medals to get cash prizes: Conade chief Rommel Pacheco announced that every medal won by Mexican athletes at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — not just an athlete’s best result, as was previously the rule — will earn a cash reward.

🥇 Payouts by medal color: Individual golds are worth 50,000 pesos, silvers 35,000 pesos and bronzes 15,000 pesos, with different amounts for team events.

🇲🇽 Best-ever CAC Games performance: Mexico won a record 407 medals (167 gold, 125 silver, 115 bronze) at the Santo Domingo Games, held July 24–Aug. 8.

⚽ Pacheco touts 2031 Women’s World Cup bid: Mexico, the U.S., Costa Rica and Jamaica are the only bidders for the 2031 tournament, and Pacheco said Mexico would be a “great host,” as it was for the recent men’s World Cup.

🇨🇴 Mexican aid en route to earthquake-hit Colombia: Two Air Force planes carrying 19.5 tonnes of humanitarian aid left for the city of Pereira on Wednesday morning, with Army troops also deploying to help.

📦 58.5 tonnes of aid by Friday: Sheinbaum said additional shipments will go out Thursday and Friday, bringing food, water and medicine to Colombia, where Monday’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake has killed at least 254 people.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The most significant information from President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference was that:

Each and every medal won by Mexican athletes at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games will be rewarded with a cash prize. Mexican humanitarian aid is on its way to Colombia, where a major earthquake on Monday caused widespread damage and significant loss of life.

Mexico’s performance at the recent Olympics-style sporting event in the Dominican Republic and its response to the temblor in Colombia underscore its position as a regional power.

Mexico — the Western Hemisphere’s third most populous country and fourth largest economy — invariably lends a hand when disaster strikes in the region. It went to Venezuela’s assistance when a powerful earthquake struck that country on June 24, while this month it sent more than 300 firefighters to British Columbia, Canada, as intense forest fires raged in the province.

All medals won by Mexicans in Dominican Republic will be rewarded with cash prizes

At the start of her press conference, Sheinbaum noted that medalists from the recently concluded Central American and Caribbean Games were in attendance.

“We’re very proud of you, of the role you played at the Central American Games, a medal record,” she said.

Medallero final de los XXV Juegos Centroamericanos y del Caribe #SantoDomingo2026 🥇🥈🥉 Felicidades a cada una de las delegaciones por una cosecha llena de esfuerzo y orgullo. ¡Nos vemos en los próximos Juegos! 💙 Final medal standings of the XXV Central American and Caribbean… pic.twitter.com/7JtZ7jjcUW — Santo Domingo 2026 (@SDQ2026) August 8, 2026

Mexico won a total of 407 medals at the 16-day event held from July 24 to Aug. 8 in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic. Mexican competitors took home 167 gold medals, 125 silver medals and 115 bronze medals.

Rommel Pacheco, director of the National Commission for Physical Culture and Sport (Conade), told reporters that Mexico’s medal haul amounted to its best ever performance at the Central American and Caribbean Games, a multi-sport event contested by more than 30 countries every four years.

“Behind every one of these medals, there were months [and] years of training,” Pacheco said.

Later in his presentation, the Conade chief announced that all medalists from the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games would receive a cash prize from the government for each and every medal they won.

“As you know, when [Mexican] athletes win medals at the Central American Games, the Pan American Games, the Olympics or World Championships, they get a scholarship and also an economic stimulus,” Pacheco said.

“… Normally, only the best medal [an athlete wins] is rewarded. But the president said to me: ‘I think we should reward all the medals.’ So the surprise is that for both athletes and trainers, all the medals will be rewarded,” he said.

Pacheco later noted that an individual gold medal is rewarded with 50,000 pesos (US $2,930), while silver and bronze medals are rewarded with 35,000 and 15,000 pesos, respectively.

“For teams it varies a little bit,” he said.

“… What’s going to happen is that all medals are going to be rewarded. For example, we have a swimmer who, on her own, won 11 medals,” Pacheco said, referring to 23-year-old Guanajuato native Celia Pulido.

Pacheco: Mexico will be a ‘great host’ of 2031 women’s World Cup

Pacheco noted that Mexico is vying to be a host of the 2031 FIFA women’s World Cup.

Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica submitted a joint bid to host the quadrennial tournament. No other bids have been submitted, meaning that it’s all but certain that the four Western Hemisphere countries will host the 2031 event.

Pacheco said that if Mexico is confirmed as a co-host of the 2031 women’s World Cup — the next edition of which will be played in Brazil next year — Mexicans will be “happy.”

Hosting a World Cup “grows the spirit of the sport,” he said.

“We will be a great host as we were with the [men’s] World Cup,” Pacheco said.

Sheinbaum: Mexican aid heading to Colombia today

Sheinbaum told reporters that the Mexican government received a specific aid request from the government of Colombia, where a 7.4 magnitude earthquake on Monday toppled buildings in various towns and cities and claimed at least 254 lives, according to a Reuters report on Wednesday morning.

She said that two Mexican Air Force planes carrying 19.5 tonnes of humanitarian aid departed the Felipe Ángeles International Airport on Wednesday morning to fly to Pereira, Colombia.

“Mexican Army troops are also obviously going to help in all the [rescue and recovery] work,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that Mexico will send more humanitarian aid to Colombia on Thursday and Friday. A total of 58.5 tonnes of Mexican aid, including food and other essential goods, will be sent to the South American country between Wednesday and Friday, Sheinbaum said.

“Water is being sent, medicine is being sent as well,” she said.

“We’re going to be in contact [with the Colombian government] … in order to provide all the support Colombia needs,” Sheinbaum said.

World.title: Buenos Aires Tango Festival 2026: Free World Mundial
World.content:
Argentina · Culture

What: Tango BA Festival y Mundial — the Buenos Aires tango festival and World Tango Championship, billed as the world’s largest tango event.

Tango BA Festival y Mundial — the Buenos Aires tango festival and World Tango Championship, billed as the world’s largest tango event. When: 19 August to 2 September 2026, opening at La Usina del Arte.

19 August to 2 September 2026, opening at La Usina del Arte. Where: More than 50 venues across the city, from the Teatro Colón to neighborhood cultural centers.

More than 50 venues across the city, from the Teatro Colón to neighborhood cultural centers. Championship: Two categories — Tango de Pista (social floor tango) and Tango Escenario (stage tango). Finals 1–2 September at the Teatro Gran Rex.

Two categories — Tango de Pista (social floor tango) and Tango Escenario (stage tango). Finals 1–2 September at the Teatro Gran Rex. Cost: Free admission to most events. Some need a reservation up to 72 hours ahead.

Free admission to most events. Some need a reservation up to 72 hours ahead. Who runs it: The Buenos Aires city government, with about 2,000 artists on the bill.

For two weeks the whole city turns into a dance floor. It is one of the best free things you can do in South America this winter.

The Buenos Aires tango festival is back, and it is the biggest one on the planet. The Tango BA Festival y Mundial opens on Wednesday 19 August 2026 and runs through 2 September. The city government puts it on every year. Most of it costs you nothing.

Buenos Aires hosts the world’s largest tango festival from 19 August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the festival actually is

Think of it as two events in one. There is the festival, with concerts, classes, and dance nights called milongas. There is also the Mundial, the World Tango Championship, where couples compete for the world title.

The 2026 edition brings around 2,000 artists to the stage. Events spread across more than 50 venues, from grand theaters to small neighborhood halls. The opening night at La Usina del Arte features singers Vicentico and Abel Pintos, backed by the city’s tango orchestra.

Why the Buenos Aires tango festival draws the world

Tango was born in Buenos Aires more than a century ago. So this is the sport’s home ground, and dancers treat winning here like a World Cup. Qualifying rounds run in Argentine provinces and in cities abroad before the finalists reach the capital.

The championship has two categories. Tango de Pista is the close, walking style you would dance at a real milonga. Tango Escenario is the showy stage version, with lifts and big choreography. Hundreds of couples from dozens of countries take part each year.

Where to go and what it costs

The short answer on price is simple. Admission to most events is free. Some popular shows and milongas ask you to book a spot online, up to 72 hours in advance, while others let you walk in until the seats run out.

Venues range from the famous to the humble. You might catch an orchestra at the Teatro Colón one night and a free class at a local cultural center the next. The championship finals land on 1 and 2 September at the Teatro Gran Rex downtown.

Why it matters if you live here or visit

August is low-season winter in Buenos Aires, so flights and hotels tend to be cheaper. A free world-class festival is a strong reason to come now rather than in summer. For anyone already living in the region, it is an easy weekend trip.

The event is also a big tourism draw for the city. Past finals have pulled huge crowds. In 2022 the city staged the closing rounds outdoors by the Obelisco, and more than 20,000 people turned up to watch. Bars, restaurants, and hotels around the venues all feel the lift.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Buenos Aires tango festival in 2026? The Tango BA Festival y Mundial runs from 19 August to 2 September 2026. It opens at La Usina del Arte and the World Championship finals fall on 1 and 2 September. Is the tango festival free? Yes, admission to most events is free. Some shows and milongas ask you to reserve a place online up to 72 hours ahead, and others are first-come, first-served. What are the World Tango Championship categories? There are two. Tango de Pista is the social, close-embrace floor style, and Tango Escenario is the stage style with lifts and choreography. Who organizes the festival? The city government of Buenos Aires runs it each year. The 2026 edition features about 2,000 artists across more than 50 venues.

Sources: Buenos Aires city tourism board (turismo.buenosaires.gob.ar); Buenos Aires city government (buenosaires.gob.ar); La Nación; Diario de Cultura; Ámbito.

World.title: Paraguay Export Boom: Sales Hit US$12.1B, Up 25%
World.content:
Paraguay · Economy

Total exports reached US$12,133.7 million from January through July 2026 — up 25.2% on the same period a year earlier, according to the Central Bank of Paraguay (BCP).

beef exports fell 7.4% to US$1,120.5 million, and electricity export volumes dropped 19.3%. Argentina was the top buyer at US$3,279.3 million (41.6% of shipments), up 52.6%, ahead of Brazil and Chile.

Soybeans, soy derivatives and cross-border factory goods pushed Paraguay’s foreign sales to a fresh high in the first seven months of the year — and flipped the trade balance back into the black.

The Paraguay export boom is real, and the official numbers now confirm it. The Central Bank of Paraguay says the country sold US$12,133.7 million worth of goods abroad between January and July 2026, a 25.2% jump on the same stretch of 2025. That is enough to turn last year’s trade gap into a solid surplus, and it puts Paraguay on track for one of its strongest trade years on record.

Soybeans and maquila drove Paraguay’s export surge. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Inside the Paraguay export boom

Start with the headline figure. The US$12,133.7 million total covers everything Paraguay ships out — not just home-grown goods. The BCP splits it three ways. Registered exports, meaning products actually made or grown in Paraguay, came to US$7,884.3 million, or about 65% of the total, and rose 20.5%. Re-exports — goods that pass through the country on their way somewhere else — added US$3,071.8 million. A third bucket the bank calls “other exports” more than doubled to US$1,177.6 million.

The trade balance tells the clearest story. Imports also grew, reaching US$11,454.6 million, up 12.8%. But exports climbed far faster than imports. That gap produced a US$679.1 million surplus. A year earlier, Paraguay was running a US$462.9 million deficit over the same months. That is a swing of more than US$1.1 billion in twelve months.

Soybeans do the heavy lifting

If you want one word for what is powering all this, it is soy. Raw soybean shipments alone brought in US$2,648.6 million, close to 50% more than a year earlier, on volumes up nearly 41%. Soybean oil added US$432.3 million (up 23.1%) and soybean meal another US$432.2 million (up 18.7%). Together, the soy complex is doing most of the work.

A good harvest and firm prices explain the surge. Primary products as a whole — the raw farm goods — rose about 40% to US$3,151.5 million. Factory goods made under Paraguay’s maquila regime, where companies assemble products for export using cheap local labor and power, climbed 32.1% to US$858.7 million. That maquila growth matters, because it shows the boom is not only about the weather and the soybean crop.

Where beef and power slipped

Not every sector joined the party, and this is worth flagging. Beef, usually one of Paraguay’s proudest exports, went the other way. Shipments fell 7.4% to US$1,120.5 million, with volumes down almost a quarter. Cattle numbers and shifting demand appear to be weighing on the sector for now.

Electricity was the other soft spot. Paraguay is a huge power producer thanks to the Itaipú and Yacyretá dams, and energy sales are often cited as a pillar of its exports. This year, though, electricity export volumes fell 19.3%, which the central bank links to higher use at home. So while soy and maquila are lifting the total, beef and power are quietly dragging — a useful reminder that headline growth can hide very different stories underneath.

Who is buying, and why it matters to you

Paraguay’s neighbors are its best customers. Argentina took US$3,279.3 million of shipments, 41.6% of the total, and its purchases jumped 52.6%. Brazil was next at US$1,995.1 million (25.3%), up a modest 3.7%. Chile came third at US$503.8 million, though its buying slipped 11.5%. In short, the Southern Cone is buying big, and Argentina in particular is back at the table.

Here is why this should matter if you live in or invest across Latin America. A country running a trade surplus tends to earn more hard currency, which supports its guaraní and helps keep inflation and interest rates steadier — part of why Paraguay keeps drawing farmers, manufacturers and remote workers looking for a low-cost, low-tax base. A strong trade year also feeds the wider economy, from trucking and ports to the small businesses that serve them. If you are weighing a move, a property purchase or a supplier in the region, Paraguay’s export strength is one more sign of an economy holding its footing while others wobble.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Paraguay export in 2026 so far? From January through July 2026, Paraguay exported US$12,133.7 million worth of goods, according to the Central Bank of Paraguay. That was 25.2% more than the same period in 2025. Is that a trade surplus or a deficit? A surplus. Exports of US$12,133.7 million outpaced imports of US$11,454.6 million, leaving a US$679.1 million surplus. A year earlier, Paraguay had a US$462.9 million deficit over the same months. What is driving the growth? Mainly soybeans and soy products, plus maquila factory goods. Raw soybean shipments alone rose close to 50%. Beef and electricity exports, by contrast, fell during the period. Who buys the most from Paraguay? Argentina is the top destination at US$3,279.3 million (41.6% of shipments), followed by Brazil at US$1,995.1 million and Chile at US$503.8 million.

Sources: Central Bank of Paraguay (BCP) foreign trade report, via ABC Color, La Nación, Última Hora and El Trueno (August 12, 2026).

World.title: Colombia Road Closures After the Quake: Which Coffee-Region Routes Are Cut, One-Laned, or Reopened
World.content:
Colombia · Travel

Key Facts — About 13 roads hit Invias counted roughly 13 national corridors closed or restricted just after the quake, and at least nine named routes were still affected on 13 August 2026.

— Fully closed Cartago-Alcala, Armenia-Alcala, Pereira-Chinchina and Cali-Loboguerrero were reported shut by landslides, along with the Alto de Letras section toward Fresno.

— Down to one lane Calarca-Cajamarca is passing traffic on a single lane at three points, and the Libertad-Fresno bridge route has about four affected kilometres.

— Reopened the Cauya-La Felisa section has been fully cleared and put back into service.

— It changes hourly check Invias and the police road pages before you leave, because openings and closures shift through the day.

The map is redrawing itself by the hour across the coffee belt. Before you drive to Pereira, Armenia or Manizales, know what is shut, one-laned, or reopened.

Coffee bushes blanket the steep hillsides of Colombia’s coffee region, the kind of mountainous terrain crossed by the roads that landslides have cut or narrowed since the 10 August 2026 earthquake. (Photo: Marrirc, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The Colombia road closures from the 10 August 2026 earthquake could reshape any drive across the coffee region. Invias counted about 13 national roads hit right after the quake.

And by 13 August 2026 many were still cut, one-laned, or only just reopening.

Why the Colombia Road Closures Matter for Your Drive

The coffee region sits in steep, wet mountains, and its main roads thread along valley walls and high passes. When the ground shakes, those slopes give way and the road underneath simply disappears.

That is what the 10 August 2026 earthquake did to more than a dozen corridors at once. Landslides, called derrumbes locally, buried lanes, cracked bridges and cut whole towns off from the main highways.

For a driver, that means a route you took last month may not exist today. This guide walks through which roads are shut, which are squeezed to one lane, and which have reopened.

How Many Roads Are Actually Affected

Invias, the national roads agency, counted about 13 corridors closed or restricted in the first reports after the quake. That figure is a snapshot, not a fixed number, and it has moved as crews clear debris.

As of 13 August 2026, at least nine named routes across the coffee belt and Valle del Cauca were still affected. Some have since reopened, and others may close again if the slopes keep slipping.

So treat any single count as rough. The useful thing is not the total but knowing the status of the exact road you plan to use.

The Routes That Are Fully Closed

Several corridors were reported completely shut by landslides. They include Cartago-Alcala, Armenia-Alcala, Pereira-Chinchina and Cali-Loboguerrero.

The Pereira-Chinchina closure sat between roughly kilometre 22 and 24, blocked by a slide. On the Manizales-Fresno road, the Alto de Letras pass was closed at the Cerro Bravo section.

A full closure means there is no way through, not a slow crawl. If your route touches one of these, you need a different road entirely, not patience.

Calarca-Cajamarca: One Lane, Three Pinch Points

The Calarca-Cajamarca corridor is the busy crossing over the central mountains near the La Linea tunnel. It stayed open, but only barely.

Crews have it passing traffic on a single lane at three separate points. That means stop-and-go control, long waits, and convoys let through one direction at a time.

You can still use it, but budget far more time than usual. Expect to sit in line while flaggers alternate the traffic through each narrow stretch.

The Libertad-Fresno Bridge Route

Over in Tolima and Caldas, the Libertad-Fresno bridge route took a string of hits. Reports describe about four affected kilometres, with several damaged points along the corridor.

Much of that stretch is moving on a single lane where it is open at all. The damage clusters around the bridge and the approaches on either side.

If you are heading between Manizales, Fresno and the Magdalena valley, this is the corridor to check first. Its status has been among the most changeable since the quake.

Cartago-Alcala and the Valle Crossings

Cartago-Alcala, linking Valle del Cauca and Quindio, was reported closed by earth movement. It is one of the clearer full closures on the list.

Nearby, Santa Cecilia-Asia in Risaralda was also flagged by Invias among the affected corridors. Reports differ on whether it is fully shut or held to one managed lane, so treat it as blocked until you confirm.

Other Valle crossings, including Cali-Loboguerrero and stretches of the Buga-Buenaventura road, were hit as well. If your trip runs west toward the Pacific, check each leg separately.

The One Piece of Good News: Cauya-La Felisa Reopened

Not everything is bad news for drivers. The Cauya-La Felisa section, closed by a slide right after the quake, has been fully cleared.

Invias reported it back in service, carrying traffic again. It is a reminder that these closures are being worked around the clock, and some do lift within days.

That is also the catch. A road open this morning can shut again by evening if the hillside above it moves.

So a reopening is good news, not a guarantee.

How to Check the Status Before You Leave

The single most useful habit right now is to check the official status the morning you travel. Invias runs a live road-status page, and the national police publish one too.

Invias posts updates on its site and its social channels, often by exact route name and kilometre. The police estado de las vias page is a good second source to cross-check.

Ask locally as well, because drivers and bus operators often know a slide before the page updates. A quick call to a hotel or a bus terminal can save you a wasted trip.

Planning a Detour

When your usual road is shut, the detour is often long, because the mountains leave few alternatives. Crossing the central range, for instance, funnels almost everyone onto the same few passes.

If Calarca-Cajamarca is crawling, some drivers wait it out rather than attempt a much longer loop. If Cartago-Alcala is closed, plan a wider route through the open Valle del Cauca roads.

Fuel up before you set off and carry water and snacks. A one-lane pass or a surprise closure can turn a two-hour drive into most of a day.

What to Expect on the Road Right Now

Even on open roads, expect slower going across the whole region for a while. Crews, machinery and loose material are common, and speed limits drop through work zones.

Drive for the conditions, not the map. Rain loosens already-fragile slopes, so mornings after a wet night are when fresh slides are most likely.

Above all, do not squeeze past barriers or drive around a closure sign. Those closures mark ground that is still moving, and the risk is real.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which roads are closed?

Corridors reported fully closed include Cartago-Alcala, Armenia-Alcala, Pereira-Chinchina and Cali-Loboguerrero. Closures shift daily, so confirm on Invias before you travel.

Can I still drive Calarca-Cajamarca?

Yes, it stayed open, but it is passing traffic on a single lane at three points. Expect long waits and stop-and-go control, and allow far more time than usual.

How do I check current status?

Use the Invias live road-status page and its official social channels, and cross-check the national police estado de las vias page. Ask locally too, since drivers often know about a slide before the pages update.

Is there a detour?

Usually yes, but the mountains make detours long, and sometimes waiting out a one-lane stretch beats a wide loop. Plan the alternative before you leave, fuel up, and carry water in case the drive stretches out.

Sources: Invias (Instituto Nacional de Vias) road-status reports; Policia Nacional estado de las vias; Semana, La FM and regional Colombian media, 10-13 August 2026.

World.title: GM Puts Paraguay at the Center of Its Regional Strategy
World.content:
Paraguay · Business

Key Facts Who and what: Thomas Owsianski, General Motors’ president and CEO for South America, has publicly ranked Paraguay among the fastest-growing car markets in the region — “and, I think, the world.”

Thomas Owsianski, General Motors’ president and CEO for South America, has publicly ranked Paraguay among the fastest-growing car markets in the region — “and, I think, the world.” Not a factory: This is a sales-and-distribution push, not a new plant or an assembly hub. GM builds its regional vehicles in Brazil (Gravataí); Paraguay remains an import market.

This is a sales-and-distribution push, not a new plant or an assembly hub. GM builds its regional vehicles in Brazil (Gravataí); Paraguay remains an import market. The bestseller: The Chevrolet S10 pickup is Paraguay’s single best-selling vehicle, at roughly 4.5% of the market, powered by the country’s farm boom.

The Chevrolet S10 pickup is Paraguay’s single best-selling vehicle, at roughly 4.5% of the market, powered by the country’s farm boom. Footprint: Chevrolet runs about 20 showrooms and 19 service centers in Paraguay; across South America GM counts around 1,000 dealers and 1,500 service points.

Chevrolet runs about 20 showrooms and 19 service centers in Paraguay; across South America GM counts around 1,000 dealers and 1,500 service points. Shift to SUVs and hybrids: SUVs now make up more than 60% of GM’s Paraguay sales; hybrid sales rose about 65% over three years, versus 25% for petrol models.

SUVs now make up more than 60% of GM’s Paraguay sales; hybrid sales rose about 65% over three years, versus 25% for petrol models. New metal: In one year Chevrolet went from two petrol SUVs to five options, including its first electric model, the Captiva EV.

A global carmaker just put one of South America’s smallest markets on its weekly radar. Here is what GM actually said — and what it does not mean.

The GM Paraguay regional strategy is getting louder, and the message is simple: a small, low-cost country is punching well above its size. Thomas Owsianski, General Motors’ president and CEO for South America, told local outlet ABC Color this week that Paraguay is “one of the markets with the highest growth in South America and, I think, the world.”

What GM actually announced

Let’s be precise, because the headline can mislead. GM is not building a car plant in Paraguay. It is not moving its regional headquarters to Asunción, and there is no new maquila factory in this story.

What GM is doing is elevating Paraguay inside its commercial playbook. Owsianski, who took the regional top job on 1 February 2026, said GM now holds weekly sales meetings with its country managers for Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia. A market of roughly seven million people is being managed alongside Brazil, a giant of more than 200 million. That is the real signal here.

GM is elevating Paraguay in its South America sales strategy. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why the GM Paraguay regional strategy leans on pickups

Follow the farms and you find the cars. Paraguay is a soy and beef exporter, and its agribusiness sector is expanding fast — which means strong demand for tough, load-carrying pickups.

The Chevrolet S10 is the payoff. Owsianski said it is Paraguay’s best-selling vehicle at about 4.5% of the market, a share that beats the model’s standing in several larger South American countries. “The segment is important, agribusiness is growing very strongly, and we have a very successful performance here,” he said.

A test track for hybrids and EVs

Paraguay is also becoming a shop window for GM’s newest technology. In the space of a year, Chevrolet went from two petrol SUVs on sale to five options, adding the S10 Trail Boss, the Onix Activ, the Sonic, the Spark and the fully electric Captiva EV.

Buyers are responding. SUVs now account for more than 60% of GM’s Paraguay sales, and hybrid sales climbed roughly 65% over three years while petrol models grew about 25%. The compact Sonic, an SUV with coupé styling built in Brazil, arrived on 1 June 2026 priced from about G 118.7 million (US$19,990).

Why a global carmaker elevates small, low-cost Paraguay

Paraguay has quietly built a reputation as one of the cheapest places to do business in South America. It offers low taxes, cheap hydroelectric power from the giant Itaípu and Yacyretá dams, membership of the Mercosur trade bloc, and a maquila regime that lets exporters assemble goods at a flat, low tax rate.

To be clear, GM did not cite those incentives as the reason for this move — its executives framed the growth around agribusiness demand and a young, dynamic market. But the wider backdrop matters. Manufacturers from textiles to auto parts have used Paraguay’s maquila rules to serve Brazil and Argentina from a low-cost base, and GM’s enthusiasm fits a broader pattern of companies discovering that this landlocked country can do a lot with a little. The South American car market as a whole is on track for around five million units this year, a level not seen in roughly a decade.

Why you should care

If you live in or invest in Latin America, this is a small but telling data point. When a company the size of GM starts managing Paraguay week by week alongside Brazil, it is a vote of confidence in a market that expats, nomads and investors have long treated as an afterthought.

For anyone on the ground, it means more choice and better service — more showrooms, hybrids and EVs, and a bigger parts-and-service network as GM competes hard against fast-arriving Chinese brands. For investors, it is a reminder that Paraguay’s low-cost, pro-business model is pulling in blue-chip names, even if the cars themselves are still stamped out across the border in Brazil.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is General Motors building a factory in Paraguay? No. Based on what GM has announced, this is a sales and distribution move, not manufacturing. GM builds its regional cars in Brazil, chiefly at the Gravataí plant, and Paraguay remains an import market served by Chevrolet showrooms and service centers. Did GM move its South America headquarters to Paraguay? No. There is no announcement of a headquarters move. GM’s regional leadership remains centered on Brazil, and Paraguay is one of several countries — alongside Brazil, Uruguay and Bolivia — managed under the same regional team. What did GM’s regional chief actually say about Paraguay? Thomas Owsianski, GM’s president and CEO for South America, called Paraguay one of the fastest-growing car markets in the region and possibly the world. He highlighted the Chevrolet S10 pickup as the country’s bestseller and the strength of agribusiness-driven demand. Why is Paraguay attractive to carmakers and investors? Paraguay offers low taxes, cheap hydroelectric energy, Mercosur trade access and a maquila regime for exporters. GM did not name these as its reasons, but they form the broader business case that keeps drawing companies to the country.

Sources: ABC Color (interview with Thomas Owsianski, 12 August 2026; Chevrolet Sonic launch, 16 May 2026); GM Authority (GM South America leadership, February 2026); Última Hora and InfoNegocios (Chevrolet dealer network, Paraguay). Guaraní converted at US$1 = PYG 5,939.

World.title: AWS AI Plan for Peru: 250,000 to Be Trained Free
World.content:
Peru · Technology

What it is: “AWS Entrena Perú,” a free online platform teaching artificial intelligence and cloud computing in Spanish.

“AWS Entrena Perú,” a free online platform teaching artificial intelligence and cloud computing in Spanish. The goal: reach 250,000 Peruvians by 2028, with sharable AWS credentials on completion.

reach 250,000 Peruvians by 2028, with sharable AWS credentials on completion. Who is behind it: Amazon Web Services and the Fundación Romero, endorsed by the U.S. Embassy in Lima.

Amazon Web Services and the Fundación Romero, endorsed by the U.S. Embassy in Lima. The catch: no dollar figure, data centre or capital commitment was disclosed — this is skills training, not committed investment.

no dollar figure, data centre or capital commitment was disclosed — this is skills training, not committed investment. The timing: launched in late June 2026, weeks before Keiko Fujimori took office on 28 July 2026.

launched in late June 2026, weeks before Keiko Fujimori took office on 28 July 2026. The gap it targets: Perú has roughly 3,700 tech vacancies but only about 2,700 qualified candidates.

Amazon’s cloud arm is betting on Peruvian talent rather than Peruvian concrete — and that distinction matters for anyone reading the headlines.

The AWS Peru AI investment plan making the rounds this summer is real, but it is worth reading closely. Amazon Web Services (AWS) is not writing Perú a cheque or breaking ground on a data centre. It is promising to train a quarter of a million people, for free, in the skills that run the modern internet.

AWS and Fundación Romero will train 250,000 Peruvians in AI and cloud skills. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What AWS actually announced

The program is called “AWS Entrena Perú.” It is a free online platform, in Spanish, that teaches the basics of artificial intelligence and cloud computing.

Amazon Web Services built it with the Fundación Romero, the social arm of one of Perú’s largest business groups. The U.S. Embassy in Lima endorsed the launch, and Ambassador Bernie Navarro appeared at the event. The stated target is to reach 250,000 Peruvians by 2028.

Two quick definitions, because the jargon does the heavy lifting here. “The cloud” simply means renting computer power and storage over the internet instead of buying your own machines. “AI adoption” means everyday businesses actually using artificial intelligence tools — not building them.

The AWS Peru AI investment plan, in plain numbers

Here is the honest framing. The AWS Peru AI investment plan is an investment in people, not in property or capital.

AWS did not disclose a spending figure. There is no announced data centre, no promised server farm, and no cloud “region” on Peruvian soil. What is on the table is coursework: modules on AI and cloud fundamentals for the general public, developer and “AI agent” tracks for students, and applied AI tools for small-business owners.

Anyone aged 18 or over can sign up at enperu.awsentrena.com. Finish a course and you get a digital credential you can post on a résumé or a professional network. The effort also folds in “Peruanas a la Nube,” a 2023 push to bring 20,000 Peruvian women into cloud work.

Why Perú has a talent hole to fill

Perú wants the jobs but lacks the workers. The country has around 3,700 open technology roles and only about 2,700 people qualified to fill them, leaving more than a thousand posts empty — many of them in AI.

The pay gap explains the urgency. According to figures cited at the launch, demand for AI skills has grown roughly 3.5 times faster than the average job since 2016, and AI-specialised roles can carry salary premiums of up to 25 percent.

Joel Vera, the AWS general manager for Perú, Ecuador and Bolivia, framed it as widening access. Martín Pérez of the Fundación Romero said the courses strengthen what the foundation already offers its scholarship recipients.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

If your money or your life is tied to the region, watch what big tech commits versus what it announces. A training program costs Amazon relatively little and buys enormous goodwill; a data centre would signal real, long-term capital betting on Peruvian electricity, land and rules.

This is the first kind, not the second. Still, it is a leading indicator. Companies rarely train a workforce in a country they plan to ignore, and a deeper pool of cloud and AI talent is exactly what would make Perú cheaper and easier to build in next.

The political backdrop adds weight. Keiko Fujimori took office on 28 July 2026 after years of churn that saw Perú cycle through roughly eight presidents in a decade, and her government inherits a national AI strategy approved earlier this year. Foreign tech that plants roots — even shallow ones — is a vote of tentative confidence in that stability.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is AWS building a data centre in Perú? No. Nothing announced here involves a data centre, a cloud region or any physical infrastructure. It is an online training program only. How much is AWS investing? AWS did not disclose a figure. The commitment is measured in people trained — 250,000 by 2028 — rather than in dollars or soles. Who can take the courses, and what do they cost? Any Peruvian aged 18 or older can enrol for free at enperu.awsentrena.com. Courses cover AI and cloud basics, with tracks for students and small-business owners, and offer credentials on completion. Did Keiko Fujimori’s government launch this? No. AWS and the Fundación Romero launched it in late June 2026, before President Fujimori took office on 28 July. The U.S. Embassy endorsed it, but it is a private-sector program.

Sources: Diario Oficial El Peruano; Infobae Perú; Andina; U.S. Embassy in Perú; Fundación Romero (Becas Grupo Romero); Proceso; Wikipedia (Elecciones generales de Perú de 2026).

World.title: Uribe Londoño Named Colombia’s Ambassador to the UK
World.content:
Colombia · Politics

Colombia’s new government has named Miguel Uribe Londoño as ambassador to the United Kingdom, with the news breaking on 13 August 2026.

He is the father of Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay, the 2026 presidential pre-candidate who was shot on 7 June 2025 and died on 11 August 2025.

The appointment comes from President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on 7 August 2026 on a hardline, right-leaning platform.

Reported diplomatic postings also include Carlos Felipe Mejía to Madrid, Jorge Jaller Jaramillo to Caracas and Mauricio Tobón to Mexico City.

Separately, the government is preparing a decree to force the retirement of public employees who already draw a recognised pension.

Vice President José Manuel Restrepo is championing the payroll move, which unions say could hit public-school teachers hardest.

A grieving political father heads to London, and a state-payroll decree takes shape — the first signals of how Colombia’s new president plans to govern.

Colombia’s new administration has moved fast on its diplomatic bench, and one name stands out: Miguel Uribe Londoño as ambassador to the United Kingdom. He is the father of Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay, the presidential hopeful who was shot at a campaign event and later died. The London posting, reported on 13 August 2026, is one of President Abelardo de la Espriella’s first high-profile appointments.

Colombia’s new president named Uribe Londoño ambassador to the UK. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What we know about the appointment

Colombian outlets including Semana, El Espectador and La República reported that de la Espriella’s government will send Uribe Londoño to London. The reports frame it as a settled decision rather than a rumour, though the government had not published the formal diplomatic paperwork as this story went out.

The timing is striking. The news landed days after an 11 August ceremony marking one year since his son’s death. At that event, Uribe Londoño said his son “chose to die rather than stay silent” and “died because he believed politics could save lives.” The London job now hands him a public role of his own.

Who is Miguel Uribe Londoño

Uribe Londoño is a veteran of Colombia’s political right. His name became widely known abroad through his son, Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay of the Centro Democrático (Democratic Centre) party.

Uribe Turbay, 39, was a pre-candidate for the 2026 presidential election. He was shot on 7 June 2025 at El Golfito Park in the Modelia area of Bogotá, and he died on 11 August 2025 from his injuries. A 15-year-old was arrested at the scene, and prosecutors later charged several more suspects, naming Elder José Arteaga Hernández as an alleged organiser of the attack. After his son’s death, Uribe Londoño launched his own presidential campaign in August 2025.

Uribe Londoño ambassador to the United Kingdom: the symbolism

Naming Uribe Londoño ambassador to the United Kingdom is more than a routine posting. It ties de la Espriella’s young government to one of the most emotive stories in recent Colombian politics.

Supporters may read it as a tribute to a family that paid a brutal price for public life. Critics may ask whether a diplomatic post tied to a grieving, high-profile political family is the best way to fill an embassy. Both readings are fair, and both are worth watching as de la Espriella fills out the rest of his team. The reports place the London appointment alongside postings to Madrid, Caracas and Mexico City, while the key Washington seat was still unannounced.

The forced-retirement decree

On a separate track, the government is preparing a decree to force the retirement of public employees who already have a recognised pension. Coverage from Semana, La República, Infobae and others describes a draft aimed at clearing pensioned staff off the state payroll to make room for younger workers.

The reported plan would not take anyone’s pension away. Instead, it would end the job while the person keeps the pension they have already earned. Under current rules, set out in Law 1821 of 2016, many public workers can stay in their posts up to age 70 and delay drawing their pension if they choose. Vice President José Manuel Restrepo is promoting the change as a way to open jobs for new generations. The teachers’ union Fecode has raised the alarm, warning that public-school teachers could be among the hardest hit. The final text, exceptions and start date had not been published, so treat the specifics as provisional.

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

If you live in Colombia or have money at work there, both moves are early tells. Ambassadors shape how easy it is to do business, travel and move capital between Colombia and a major partner like the UK, so who sits in London is not just symbolic. The retirement decree, meanwhile, touches the size and cost of the state payroll, a line that ratings agencies and bond investors read closely. Watch how the courts and unions respond, because a decree like this can be challenged — and how de la Espriella handles that fight will tell you a lot about the next four years.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is being named Colombia’s ambassador to the United Kingdom? Colombian media report that President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government is sending Miguel Uribe Londoño to London as ambassador. The news broke on 13 August 2026. How is he connected to Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay? He is the senator’s father. Miguel Uribe Turbay, a 39-year-old presidential pre-candidate, was shot on 7 June 2025 in Bogotá and died on 11 August 2025. What would the forced-retirement decree do? As reported, it would remove public employees who already hold a recognised pension from their jobs, while letting them keep that pension. The government presents it as a way to bring in younger staff. Has any of this been made fully official? Not entirely. As this story went out, the government had not published the formal ambassador paperwork or the final decree text, so some details could still change.

Sources: Semana; El Espectador; La República; Pulzo; La FM; Infobae; El Heraldo; Wikipedia (Assassination of Miguel Uribe Turbay); CNN.

World.title: Cash Deposits in Mexico: The 15,000-Peso Line That Quietly Flags Your Account
World.content:
Mexico · Expats

Key Facts — The threshold cash deposits over 15,000 pesos (about US$880) in one month at one bank are reported to the SAT.

— Cash only it covers peso cash and cashier’s cheques bought with cash, nothing else.

— Transfers excluded SPEI, TEF and ordinary bank transfers do not count toward the total.

— The bank reports your bank files the monthly declaration, not you, by the 17th of the following month.

— A report, not a tax crossing the line triggers an information report to the SAT, not an automatic charge.

It sounds alarming, but it is not a cap on your money. It is only the line where your bank quietly reports the total to the tax office.

A historic Mexican ten-peso banknote issued by the Republica Mexicana. In Mexico today, cash deposits above 15,000 pesos a month at a single bank are reported to the SAT, though this is a reporting threshold, not a tax. (Photo: Gobierno de Mexico, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)

In Mexico, cash deposits above 15,000 pesos in a single month at one bank are reported to the tax authority, the SAT. It is a reporting line, not a limit, and it targets cash over the counter, not transfers.

Why This Matters for Newcomers

If you have just moved to Mexico, you may pay for a lot in cash while your accounts settle in. Exchanging dollars or euros and topping up your account is completely normal.

The catch is a quiet reporting rule that most newcomers never hear about. It watches how much cash, not how much money overall, lands in your account each month.

Knowing where the line sits lets you use cash freely without raising a flag. Nothing here is illegal; it is about being seen clearly by the tax office.

A little awareness now saves an awkward conversation with your bank later.

How Cash Deposits Are Reported

Under Mexican rules, banks track the cash deposits that flow into each customer’s accounts. When the monthly total at one institution passes 15,000 pesos, the bank notes it.

That figure is close to US$880 at recent exchange rates. It is an aggregate for the whole month, not a single-transaction ceiling.

The bank then lists the account in a monthly report to the SAT. You do not fill in anything or receive a bill because of it.

What Counts Toward the 15,000 Pesos

The threshold captures physical cash handed over at a branch or an ATM. Peso banknotes and coins you deposit all add to the running total.

Cashier’s cheques bought with cash count as well, since they stand in for the cash itself. The rule looks through the instrument to the money behind it.

Everything is added up across your accounts at the same bank. Spreading cash between two accounts at one institution does not reset the count.

The total is measured per bank, so accounts at different banks are tallied separately.

Why Transfers Do Not Count

Money that arrives electronically is treated differently. A SPEI transfer, a TEF payment or an ordinary bank wire is not a cash deposit.

So a salary, a transfer from your home country or a payment from a client does not touch the 15,000-peso figure. Only cash and cash-bought cashier’s cheques do.

This is good news for anyone paid digitally. You can receive large transfers every month and never come near the reporting line.

Who Actually Files the Report

The obligation sits with the bank, not with you. Financial institutions file a monthly declaration of cash deposits to the SAT.

The current deadline is the 17th day of the month after the deposits. Your bank handles the paperwork in the background.

You will usually never know a report was sent. It is a routine data feed, not a warning or a penalty.

Millions of ordinary deposits are reported this way every month across Mexico.

A Report, Not a Tax

Crossing 15,000 pesos in cash does not create a tax bill. The report is information, telling the SAT that cash of a certain size moved through your account.

It is also not a limit on what you may deposit. Depositing more is entirely legal; it simply gets reported.

The SAT can compare the cash against your declared income and profile. Problems arise only if large cash sums have no plausible explanation.

For most people, a reported deposit simply passes by without any follow-up at all.

Where the Rule Comes From

This is longstanding Mexican law, not a new measure aimed at foreigners. It grew out of the old cash-deposit tax known as the IDE.

That tax ran from 2008 until it was repealed after 2013. When the tax disappeared, the reporting duty behind it stayed in place.

Today the obligation lives in the income tax law, in Article 55. Banks report the data even though the separate cash-deposit tax is gone.

How an Expat Can Trip the Line

The typical trap is exchanging foreign cash and then depositing it. Change US$1,000 into pesos, add it to your account, and you are already over the line.

Paying a rent deposit or buying a car in cash can push you across too. A single large cash deposit is enough on its own.

None of this is wrong, and none of it triggers a fine by itself. It only means the deposit becomes visible to the tax authority.

The fix is not to avoid cash, but to be ready to explain it.

Practical Steps to Stay Clear

Where you can, move money by transfer rather than cash. Transfers keep large sums off the cash-reporting total entirely.

If you must deposit cash, keep a simple record of where it came from. An exchange-house receipt or a withdrawal slip answers the obvious question.

Match your banking to the profile you have given the SAT. Cash that fits your stated income rarely draws a second look.

The Bottom Line for Foreigners

The 15,000-peso rule is a reporting threshold, not a wall around your money. Cross it and your bank simply tells the SAT.

Cash and cash-bought cashier’s cheques count; transfers do not. The bank files the report, and no tax is due just for passing the line.

For a foreigner settling in, the lesson is calm and practical. Use cash when you need to, keep your receipts, and lean on transfers for big sums.

Frequently Asked Questions

What counts toward the 15,000?

Physical peso cash you deposit at a branch or ATM, plus cashier’s cheques bought with cash. It is totalled across your accounts at the same bank each month.

Do transfers count?

No. SPEI, TEF and ordinary bank transfers are not cash deposits, so they do not add to the 15,000-peso figure.

Will I be taxed?

No. Passing the threshold triggers an information report to the SAT, not an automatic tax or fine on the deposit.

What should I do?

Prefer transfers for large sums and keep receipts for any big cash deposit. Cash that matches your declared income rarely raises concern.

Sources: El Informador; SAT (Servicio de Administracion Tributaria); Ley del Impuesto sobre la Renta, Article 55.

World.title: Colombia’s Power and Water After the Quake: What to Expect at Home
World.content:
Colombia · Expats

Key Facts — Power nearly back outages fell from about 70% of demand to around 11% in Valle del Cauca, and from about 82% to about 14% in Caldas, Quindío and Risaralda.

— Days from normal the grid operator XM reports about 99% of national demand restored, and Andesco says full electricity service is only days off.

— Water uncertain there is no date yet for full water and sewerage service to come back.

— Why water is slower buried pipes can crack unseen in a quake and must be checked segment by segment before the taps are certified safe.

— Where the coffee departments of Caldas, Quindío and Risaralda, plus Valle del Cauca and Cali, were hit hardest.

The good news travels faster than the bad: the grid is almost whole again. While engineers walk the water network pipe by pipe before they will promise a single safe tap.

Illustrative photo: high-voltage transmission lines. After Colombia’s earthquake of Monday, 10 August 2026, the national grid operator reported about 99% of electricity demand restored, while water and sewerage service still had no timetable. (Photo: PumpkinSky, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
