World.title: ‘That wasn’t my son’: Mother of Berlin Pride attacker confronts his turn to terror
World.content:
In the wake of the devastating events of July 25, Abdul Ballout's mother tries to reconcile the son she knew with what authorities have established about his radicalization.

The woman whose son brought terror to Berlin is sitting on a worn red leather couch in a three-room apartment in Berlin’s Tiergarten district. It is Thursday afternoon, and she is pointing to the several missed calls on her phone screen.

They are all from the evening of July 25. They are all from the same person: Abdul Ballout, her son.

“He was terribly afraid for me,” she says quietly, her voice trembling. “I didn’t know why.”

She scrolls through the call log — the last traces of her child from the day of the attack, the day the unknown 21-year-old became the most wanted man in Germany.





She wants the public to get to know him — the son, the brother, the young man that she knew. “I find the way people talk about him incredibly painful, to be honest,” she says. “He was a good person.”

These are the subjective recollections of a mother who cannot and will not accept what her son did — and whose account is difficult to reconcile with what authorities established about him both before and after the attack.

She asks that her name not be published, nor any photograph or recording of her voice.

“I have two other children I have to think about,” she says.

* * *

On the evening of July 25, Ballout drove a rented van into a crowd on the fringes of Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade.

After coming to a stop, he got out of the car and, according to authorities, began attacking people with a machete before fleeing on foot. One person was killed, and at least 29 were injured.

Around 20 hours later, special forces tracked Ballout to a garden in suburban Spandau, where he allegedly attempted to attack officers with a knife when they tried to arrest him. Police opened fire, and Ballout was shot dead. Nine days later, he was buried at Gatow Cemetery in Berlin.

A digital display on a bus stop in Berlin shows the photo of Abdul Ballout on July 26, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The person killed in Ballout’s attack was a 65-year-old woman from Poland who had traveled to Berlin with her daughter specifically for Christopher Street Day.

Not far away, a gay refugee from Iraq was celebrating at an electronic music event when panic spread through the streets. He had fled a country where being openly gay could put his life at risk. Germany was supposed to be different.

Granted anonymity to speak openly, he said: “For many people, freedom is something they never have to think about. For me, it means being able to love someone, to leave the house in the morning without wondering whether I could be attacked or killed for who I am.”

After the attack, he said, that feeling of safety cracked. “That old fear was suddenly back.”

Sitting across from me just weeks later, Ballout’s mother is dressed in all black, her headscarf framing a face that looks exhausted. There are deep shadows beneath her eyes. She speaks so quietly that at times I have to lean in to hear. The only other sound in the room is the monotonous hum of a fan.





On the coffee table lay empty coffee cups, an open packet of TUC crackers and a box of iron tablets. Propped between them is a framed photograph of Ballout, a faint grin on his face.

She doesn’t want to begin our conversation with the attack; she wants to start with her son. She reaches for her phone and starts showing me videos. In one, he is a little boy in swim trunks, running along a beach and laughing. In another, he is an adult, dancing exuberantly through the living room with his family. He jumps onto the couch and pulls his sisters along, making everyone laugh.

His mother talks of evenings spent together watching television or playing Monopoly, how he would sometimes cheat if he were about to lose. As she speaks, her smiles give way to tears, and her tears give way to smiles.

The contrast with the image of the terrorist could hardly be greater.

* * *

Four days before our interview, I visited the neighborhood where Ballout grew up. Children were crisscrossing a courtyard, neighbors leaning out of windows or standing outside doorways. I asked them about him.

All their answers were strikingly similar: “He always said hello;” “he was polite;” “he was helpful.”

No one disputed what Ballout did. No one tried to excuse it. And yet, no one could explain how the young man they knew was capable of such an act.

German police stand near a white van used in the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

Sitting in his mother’s living room a few days later, her phone rings, and for a brief moment, Arabic singing fills the room. “That’s his voice,” she says. Her ringtone is a recording of her son reciting an Islamic prayer.

But is it just an innocuous recording?

Court records show Ballout repeatedly posted videos containing Islamic State propaganda dating back to 2024, before starting to circulate recordings of his own. In some of the audio files obtained by WELT, which is — like POLITICO — part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters network, he recited the Quran; in others, he appeared to preach. He had hundreds of followers on TikTok and Telegram, with comments praising his voice.

But Ballout’s online messages were radical, speaking of “unbelievers,” God’s “agonizing punishment,” and his rejection of democracy and the German legal system.





Online, he went by the name Abu Muawiyah — a reference to the first caliph of the Umayyad dynasty who emerged victorious over the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law Ali and his followers, from which Shiite Islam later emerged. It is also a signal of his shifting faith, as Ballout converted from Shiite to Sunni Islam in 2021.

Was this also a break with his family? His mother gives no indication it was.

She speaks calmly about religion, and without hesitation. She says she was born in Beirut and grew up in Germany. She can neither read nor write Arabic and has therefore never read the Quran in its original language.

German policemen scan the ground of Tiergarten park, near the scene of the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

“I’m not particularly strict about religion,” she says. But her son was different.

For the last several years, he had increasingly been trying to push her toward stricter observance, urging her to pray regularly, to take her religious obligations more seriously and to engage more deeply with Islam.

“He told me every single day how important it was to pray and that it was my duty.”

* * *

Speaking about the days leading up to the attack, one word keeps coming up in our conversation: fear.

Her son had changed, she says. He seemed more nervous, more tense, more restless. He had started changing his phone number constantly — at least five times in 10 days.

“Why are you changing your number again?” she had asked him. But his answer was always roughly the same. Some people kept calling him; he felt followed, harassed and no longer safe.





To this day, it makes no sense to his mother. But to investigators, this is the behavior of someone who had realized he was on their radar — and was planning something big.

In late May 2026, Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office classified Ballout as a high-risk individual capable of committing a serious act of politically motivated violence. And the reasons for this are documented across dozens of pages of case files.

In 2021, Ballout took part in street dawah events organized by a Salafist group in Berlin, where Islamists seek new followers and often distribute copies of the Quran. This is where Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office first took an interest in him.

From 2023 onward, he increasingly frequented mosques influenced by Salafist ideology — which espouses an ultraconservative, fundamentalist view of Sunni Islam — while investigators noted he began openly expressing his rejection of Germany’s free democratic order.

Flowers and candles lie at a makeshift memorial in Tiergarten park on July 27, 2026, two days after the attack. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

In the summer of 2024, he repeatedly posted propaganda from the Islamic State organization, and in May 2025, attempted to join the terrorist group in Africa but was refused entry into Mauritania. Shortly after, he tried to travel to Syria via Lebanon to receive weapons training, communicating with IS members through Telegram.

Lebanese authorities arrested Ballout in July 2025, and a military court sentenced him to three months in prison for incitement to religious conflict. In court, he spoke of two cousins on his father’s side who had died fighting in Syria.

Returning to Germany in November 2025, Ballout was then arrested at Berlin airport and taken into custody on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. According to the case files, he presented himself as a preacher in prison. His religious fervor intensified, and his appearance changed. Ballout’s father later told Der Spiegel that he had argued with his son over his long hair and beard, which he regarded as a sign of religious extremism.





Finally, in May of this year, Ballout was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison but was initially released under the supervision of a probation officer while the court deferred its verdict on whether to suspend the sentence. This judicial decision is now at the center of a heated debate in Germany over how the country handles high-risk Islamist offenders.

From then on, police kept him under surveillance.

Did his mother know any of this? She shakes her head.

* * *

There is only one incident Ballout’s mother is willing to discuss: July 2 this year, his birthday. That day, she says, showed just how closely her son was being monitored.

Ballout had been playing outside with his sister, spraying her with a water gun, she says. Shortly afterward, officers from the State Criminal Police Office appeared. They had assessed the situation as a possible threat.

But investigators describe the scene differently.

It was already dark, and Ballout had stepped outside for just a few seconds, holding what appeared to be a handgun but was difficult to identify, they said. He tucked it into his waistband and went back inside. When officers eventually searched the apartment, they found only a toy gun.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks at the Marienkirche church in Berlin on July 26, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

Investigators believe the 21-year-old was testing whether he was under surveillance — and how much time he had before police would intervene.

And while his mother insists she noticed nothing that would suggest Ballout was preparing an attack, she does not rule out the possibility that others knew of her son’s plans. However, she gives no names.

He spent most of his time with family, she says. He had few friends, at least no one she knew particularly well.

* * *

The day of the attack began, in her memory, just like any other. Both mother and son slept in late, then ran errands. Ballout was unemployed and had no particular obligations, she says. In the late afternoon, he left the apartment before a family gathering that evening.

Then, suddenly, the calls started piling up.

At 5:10 p.m., Ballout called his mother. An hour later, he called again. Then again. Each time, she says, the conversation revolved around the same question: “Are you okay?” He had never done that before.





Then, after one of the calls, she received a short message: “Take care of yourself.”

The words still haunt her today.

At 7:05 p.m., Ballout called again. He asked that his mother inform her partner of over two years that he had a new phone number again. Ballout’s parents have been divorced for three years, but Ballout continued to see and speak with his father regularly, she says. And as the family prepared for the evening, the phone kept ringing.

They were supposed to have dinner at his sister’s place. Schnitzel, his favorite meal, was on the menu. Ballout loved these family gatherings, his mother says. “They always made him happy.” That is precisely why so much of what happened next is incomprehensible to her.

Police investigation marks on the ground near the scene of the attack. | Filip Singer/EPA

“He wanted to live,” she says, her voice rough.

He had spoken of the future, about having a family of his own, about all the things that still lay ahead of him. Nothing had suggested this might be a farewell.

Shortly before 10 p.m., her partner received one more call. They were the last words Ballout deliberately addressed to his family: “Get my mother to safety.”

Minutes later, the van drove into the crowd.

* * *

By the time Ballout’s mother was driven home by her partner that night, the first reports of the attack had started to circulate. At that point, she still didn’t know exactly what had taken place. But when she entered the apartment, she says, something immediately caught her attention.

A key was still in the door.

And right beside it, on the hallway shoe cabinet, were documents that seemed to be deliberately placed where they could not be overlooked. It was the rental agreement for a small van. It listed Ballout as the renter.





“That was when I knew immediately that it couldn’t mean anything good,” she says.

That same night, she took the documents to the police. And as she was questioned, a picture slowly started to emerge — one she initially refused to accept.

At the same time, she kept trying to reach her son, sending message after message. But there was no reply. She only learned the truth the next day, when her daughters called and told her about the reports on the news.

Her son was dead.

Since then, she has spent hour after hour in her Berlin apartment searching for explanations, her thoughts circling endlessly around her son’s last words, his fear and whether there may have been something in those calls that she failed to recognize. She cannot let go of the distorted image she has of her son, of the good boy who wanted to start a family.





Asked what she would say to the victims of the terrorist attack, she thinks for a long time. She is sorry, she eventually says.

“I would also tell them that wasn’t my son.”

Additional reporting by Lennart Pfahler.

Julia Zabert is a trainee journalist with the Global Reporters Network at the Axel Springer Academy. The Academy trains the next generation of leading journalists through hands-on, innovative work with a clear focus on the future of journalism. More information at axelspringeracademy.com.

World.title: Víctor Coyote dies: a life impossible to confine to music, comics and film
World.content:
Few labels ever really fitted Víctor Coyote, and that was always his best calling card. Born in Tui in 1958, he died this Thursday in a cycling accident, leaving behind a career that began in late-seventies punk and ended, close to the age of seventy, without him ever stopping reinventing himself.

 

His musical career began in 1979 with the founding of Los Coyotes, the band he fronted together with Fernando Gilabert and from which he took his stage name. The group was born out of psychobilly, but soon shifted towards Latin rhythms, becoming pioneers of that sonic crossover in Spain long before others popularised it.

Their first album, 'Mujer y sentimiento' (1985), put them on the map of the movida, a scene straddling Vigo and Madrid in which Víctor Coyote was one of the most restless figures. The band changed its name in 1988 to Los Coyotes de Víctor Abundancia and released one of its most memorable tracks, 'Esta noche me voy a bailar', before finally splitting up in 1992.

Videos, comics and Xabarín Clun

The band’s break-up did not mean a pause but a change of format. Víctor Coyote had already spent years combining music with comics, contributing to the magazine 'Madriz' between 1984 and 1987, and he threw himself fully into directing music videos and drawing.

He directed the video for 'Milonga' by Los Rodríguez, and for 'Carmiña Vacaloura', a song that was part of the soundtrack of Xabarín Club and is still lodged in the memories of much of a generation of Galicians. At the same time he published comic monographs such as 'Come yuca' (1998) and took part in collective publications that confirmed his place on Spain’s graphic scene.

A solo career impossible to pigeonhole

In 1995 he returned to the studio on his own with 'Lo bueno, dentro, disco', from which came 'Jaguarundi', that year’s theme tune for the Vuelta a España. From then on he kept releasing music, drawing and filming, never tying himself to a single medium.

In a recent interview he described his work as that of someone with "more eye than ear", and in 2024, when presenting his comic 'Si te falta calle', he explained that humour was an inevitable ingredient in his work, though never the only one: to reflect life, he said, always requires a bit of it.

Víctor Coyote did not stop working or appearing in public in his final years. Last May he acted as a guide to his own trajectory in an interview, and he was a leading figure at the Festival de Cans, revisiting eight of his most remembered works. His death this Thursday, in a cycling accident, brings to an abrupt close a career that, right to the end, refused to stay still in a single line of work.

World.title: Survivors tell of horror of Zimbabwe ferry sinking as police say death toll hits 46
World.content:
A man who survived a ferry disaster that claimed at least 46 lives on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba told the AFP news agency on Thursday how he watched helplessly as people tried to save themselves, with his best friend and seven of his relatives among the dead.

 

The overloaded government ferry, a vital link for villagers and fish traders around the vast lake, overturned in choppy waters on Tuesday in one of the country's worst passenger boat disasters.

"Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top," Chance Siyamavhu said at a memorial service in the lakeside town of Kariba close to the border with Zambia.

Perched on the upended boat, he watched as passengers struggled to survive, unable to save them.

Mourners gather for a memorial service for the victims of a ferry capsized on lake Kariba in Kariba, 13 August, 2026 AP Photo

"When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the life jackets but most of them did not even know how to use them," the 45-year-old told AFP. "Most people could not make it."

"Our relatives were swept in another direction and they sank because we were not in a position to help them," he said.

Dozens of mourners gathered in front of 44 coffins at the emotional service, as police announced that the death toll had risen to 46.

"The names of the victims who perished in the accident will be released in due course," a police statement said.

Officials say the boat was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.

A view of Kariba Port where a ferry capsized, 13 August, 2026 AP Photo

The civil protection unit said 77 people were rescued and there were fears that other passengers may be unaccounted for.

Survivors said they had pleaded for the captain to turn back as the boat took on water.

Anymore Chambati, who had been a security official on the vessel, told AFP he had tried to hand out life jackets as the boat began to sink.

"I managed to only give not more than 10," he said. "The ferry engines were filled with water because of the heavy winds and eventually they failed, save for one."

World.title: In Paris, tourists increasingly choose cycling to explore the city
World.content:
In recent years, Paris has turned itself into the world capital of cycling. This shift allows French and foreign tourists to discover certain sights and monuments in a whole new way.

 

Last June, Paris welcomed around 3.8 million tourists, about 3% more than over the same period in 2025, according to the tourist office.

And as visitor numbers rise, more and more travellers are choosing the bicycle rather than the bus or walking to get around.

"Since Covid, cycling in Paris has really taken off. Many more people want to go on bike tours and hire bikes. It has become a hugely popular way of discovering the city", says Michaël Tosello, who runs guided bike tours in Paris and points out that many routes outside the capital have also been created. And with good reason: cycle paths now link Paris to London, Mont-Saint-Michel or Spain via the Scandibérique.

"It's wonderful"

To meet this growing demand for cycling tourism, numerous companies have sprung up. Notre-Dame, Concorde, Champs-Élysées, Eiffel Tower... they offer comprehensive excursions that let visitors tour the city in just a few hours.

For Jean-Baptiste Blondiaux, a bike guide, this is the most appealing option because it allows people to see more places. "In ten minutes by bike, you can see two different monuments. On foot, that's impossible", he says. "You can see a lot more in Paris, I think. And you can see the city, the people walking and lots of things between stops. That's why it's so interesting, I think."

For the Buss family, from the United States, the bike was the perfect option given how little time they have to visit the capital. "It feels good just to be in the moment. And you can come back later and look at things a second time and have a bit more time to absorb the history and the culture of it all", says Jamie Buss, who is visiting with her husband and their three children aged 22, 18 and 16.

The family is on a 12-day trip around Europe. After a week in Tenerife, they arrived in Paris and opted for a three-hour guided tour of the French capital. "It's an excellent way to discover the city. It's hard to take everything in. But with JB's explanations [the guide, editor's note] and the fact that we're outdoors while doing all this, it's wonderful", says the father, Mike Buss.

Today, the capital has more than 1,000 km of cycle lanes. But city hall is aiming higher: in the long term, Paris is expected to have around 1,500 km of infrastructure to make the city even more accessible to soft mobility.

World.title: Ukraine needs 5% of US Patriot stocks just to get through winter, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling on Washington to release a portion of the US Patriot interceptor stockpile, saying Ukraine needs 5% of the missiles simply to get through the winter and “save people’s lives.”

 

"If they sell us 5% we will go through the winter and save people’s lives. If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles," Zelenskyy said in an interview with CNN.

Kyiv currently only has 1% of what it needs, he said.

“From one percent to five percent, I have some months and millions (of) phone calls and anything else.”

Pressed on whether the US had responded to the request, he hinted at undisclosed diplomatic efforts.

"I do some things which I can't even share. It doesn't mean it's out of the law. But I can't speak about it.”

Ukraine has no more interceptors

The appeal comes as Russia has stepped up its bombardment of Kyiv, launching mass missile attacks roughly once a week that have killed civilians and destroyed homes.

In one such strike earlier this month, Ukrainian air defences failed to bring down a single one of the 28 ballistic missiles fired at the city.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine now has "two-and-a-half times less interceptors than we had in 2025," even as "Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before."

Rescue workers try to put out a fire of a residential building and cars burning after a Russian air guided bomb strike in Zaporizhzhia, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

Ballistic missiles are significantly harder to intercept than cruise missiles or drones because of their speed and steep flight path and Kyiv's stock of Patriot interceptors has been squeezed since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in the end of February, diverting supplies of the systems elsewhere.

Russia fired more than 450 missiles at Ukraine last month, nearly 200 of them on ballistic trajectories, part of a bombardment the UN has called the deadliest for civilians since the 2022 full-scale invasion began.

World.title: People evacuated from beach as wildfire tears through popular Greek tourist hotspot
World.content:
A large wildfire broke out in Siviri in Greece's northern Halkidiki region, prompting an evacuation order via a 112 alert.

 

Firefighting numbers on the ground are being constantly reinforced and nine aircraft and seven helicopters are operating from the air, while water tankers from the Municipality of Kassandra are also assisting in efforts to contain the blaze.

A total of 110 firefighters are taking part in the firefighting operation, along with three teams from the 2nd EMODE Special Forest Operations Unit and 33 fire engines.

The forces deployed also include 12 firefighters from Moldova with three vehicles, who are in Greece as part of the European programme for the pre-positioning of firefighting resources.

Shortly after 16:30 local time the flames reached the first houses in Siviri.

After the initial 112 warning to residents and those close to the fire front, a second alert followed, calling for the evacuation of citizens from the wider area around the settlement of Siviri in the direction of Kassandreia. At the same time, an evacuation order was also issued for the settlement of Fourka.

Firefighters operate during a wildfire near Porto Germeno, 2 August, 2026 AP Photo

Evacuation of residents by sea

Shortly after 17:00 local time, the Hellenic Coast Guard, with the assistance of private boats, began evacuating people from the beach of Siviri.

Two Coast Guard vessels and nine private craft are at the scene, while the Speedrunner Jet high-speed ferry has also arrived to assist.

A ban on the movement of pedestrians and all types of vehicles, due to the high risk of wildfires, is being put in place in forest areas of the Municipalities of Kassandra, Sithonia and Aristotle, by decision of the deputy regional governor of Halkidiki, Giannis Koufidis.

The ban is expected to be in force from 8 am-8 pm on 14 August in several areas of the Municipalities of Kassandra and Sithonia.

A firefighter stands as flames rising during a wildfire near Porto Germeno, 2 August, 2026 AP Photo

To enforce the measure, checks will be carried out at the entrances to forest roads with the assistance of the police and those present in the above areas will be removed, with the exception of members of volunteer organisations taking part in the fire protection actions of the Regional Unit of Halkidiki.

The Regional Unit of Halkidiki is appealing to residents and visitors to comply with the ban and follow the instructions of the competent authorities, contributing to the protection of human life, forest ecosystems and public property.

Violating the order carries an administrative fine of €300, in accordance with current legislation.

World.title: One dead, several injured in Rotterdam port blast at Gunvor refinery
World.content:
Several injured people were taken to hospital, according to police, while forensic investigators and the Dutch labour inspectorate were sent to the scene. A damaged wall and signs of an explosion on a storage tank could be seen in the area as emergency services secured the site. Police spokesperson Daan Valkenburg said investigators were considering all possible causes and had not yet reached a conclusion.

 

The facility is operated by Gunvor Energy, which runs a refinery and fuel terminal in the sprawling port. Dutch broadcaster NOS reported that a maintenance team had been working on a section of pipes when the explosion occurred, but authorities did not confirm that account.

A separate power failure also affected another part of the port on Thursday, with a transformer catching fire, prompting several companies to halt operations and evacuate workers. Emergency services later said the blackout was not linked to the explosion. Police said the investigation would establish what happened.

World.title: Bomb hidden in bin kills Russian officer in occupied Sevastopol, Moscow says
World.content:
A bomb hidden in a rubbish bin tore through a residential street in occupied Sevastopol on Thursday morning, killing a Russian serviceman in what Moscow's security service called a Ukrainian-directed attack, the latest in a series of strikes against military figures tied to the war.

 

The explosion struck a stairwell area on Stoletovsky Avenue as the victim was walking with a companion, according to witness accounts carried by Russian Telegram channels.

Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) later confirmed that a Defence Ministry serviceman had been killed, without naming him and said it had detained a Russian woman born in 1994 whom it accused of acting on instructions from Ukrainian intelligence.

Several Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels have identified the dead man as Robert Shageev, a former captain in Ukraine's navy who commanded the submarine “Zaporizhzhia” before defecting to Russia during the 2014 annexation of Crimea.

A view of Lubyanskaya Square with the historical Federal Security Service building in Moscow, 12 July, 2023 AP Photo

According to these reports, he rose to deputy commander of the Black Sea Fleet's 4th Submarine Brigade and later took charge of the vessel “Stary Oskol,” one of the Kalibr cruise-missile carriers Russia has used against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

Kyiv has charged him with treason, though his identity remains officially unconfirmed and Ukrainian authorities have made no public comment on Thursday's blast.

The killing extends a series of attacks on Russian commanders and collaborators, both in occupied Ukrainian territory and inside Russia itself, widely attributed to partisan networks aligned with Kyiv.

On 1 August, an explosion at Moscow's Balzi Rossi restaurant reportedly targeted Alexander Chayko, commander of Russia's Aerospace Forces.

World.title: When the earth moves: six major earthquakes of 2026
World.content:
Colombia, Venezuela, Mindanao: Thousands have died in powerful earthquakes this year. Six such events show that the magnitude of the quake is not the only factor determining the scale of the disaster.

Is 2026 a particularly bad year for earthquakes? The number of extremely strong quakes so far this year is not, in fact, unusual. Over the long term, around the world, there are an average of about 15 earthquakes per year registering above magnitude 7 on the Richter scale. By mid-August this year, there had been 10. The devastation some of the quakes have wreaked has, however, been striking.

Venezuela: two quakes in just 39 seconds

On June 24, Venezuela was hit by an earthquake that proved to be by far the deadliest this year. A magnitude 7.2 quake was followed just 39 seconds later by an even stronger one of magnitude 7.5. The north of the country and the capital, Caracas, were the areas worst affected.

Two earthquakes wreaked destruction in Catia La Mar, Venezuela Image: Maxwell Briceno/AFP

According to official figures, more than 6,300 people were killed in the double earthquake. The effects on the impoverished country's infrastructure have also been dramatic. Shortly afterward, a satellite-based assessment by researchers at Oregon State University provisionally concluded that more than 58,000 buildings may have been damaged or destroyed.

Venezuela quakes death toll rises to almost 4,000 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Philippines: the strongest quake of the year

With a magnitude of 7.8, the earthquake on June 8 off the southern coast of the Philippine island of Mindanao was the strongest of 2026 so far. It occurred at a depth of about 57 kilometers (35 miles), and was felt across large parts of the island.

This university building in General Santos City on Mindanao in the Philippines collapsed during the earthquake in June Image: Daniel Ceng/Anadolu/picture alliance

At least 107 people were killed. But the fact that, despite the very high magnitude of the quake, far fewer people died in the Philippines than in Venezuela demonstrates that the strength of the quake does not necessarily determine the severity of the consequences.

Colombia: hundreds dead, despite the depth

On August 10, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colombia. The epicenter was in the Choco region, near San Jose del Palmar. Although the quake occurred at a depth of 100 kilometers (62 miles), the damage it caused was immense.

Pereira, in the foothills of the Andes, was one of the cities worst hit by the earthquake in Colombia Image: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP

More than 250 people are currently estimated to have died. Landslides and damaged roads are hampering the search for victims buried beneath the rubble, as well as the provision of supplies to remote areas. After Venezuela, this quake is the most consequential so far this year for Latin America.

Tonga: powerful earthquake with little damage

On March 24, the earth shook near the island group of Vava'u in the Pacific kingdom of Tonga. With a magnitude of 7.5, it was one of the strongest globally this year. But because there was no severe damage and no deaths, it received almost no attention from the media.

Tonga is located on the Pacific Ring of Fire and suffers frequent natural disasters, as here, after a volcanic eruption in 2022 Image: New Zealand Defence Force/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

The quake occurred unusually far below the earth's crust, at a depth of around 230 kilometers (143 miles), meaning that the tremors were significantly weakened by the time they reached the surface. To date, there have been no reports of deaths, or damage to infrastructure.

Japan: strong undersea quake off the Sanriku Coast

On April 20, there was an undersea quake off the northeastern coast of Japan. The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 7.4.

This region, the Sanriku Coast area in Iwate prefecture, achieved terrible notoriety after the catastrophic earthquake and tsunami there in 2011, which also resulted in the Fukushima nuclear disaster. A tsunami warning was issued after this year's earthquake, too, but fortunately the region was spared the devastation of that magnitude 9 quake 15 years ago.

After the earthquake off Japan's Sanriku Coast, people were evacuated as a precaution Image: Haruki Kobayashi/AP Photo/picture alliance

There was no major tsunami this time, but the quake illustrated once again how much Japan is affected by its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire. This 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) volcanic belt runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean where several tectonic plates collide.

Afghanistan: weak, but deadly

The earthquake in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhsham on April 3 only reached a magnitude of 5.8, which puts it right at the bottom of the list of the strongest earthquakes this year. Despite this, at least 12 people were killed, which is why it counts as one of the most significant quakes of 2026.

Poor building construction contributed to the deaths of several people in a magnitude 5.8 earthquake in Afghanistan in April Image: Saifurahman Safi/Xinhua/IMAGO

In poorer countries, even slight tremors can have deadly consequences. The risks are heightened by inadequate building construction, the difficulty of accessing remote areas and underdeveloped disaster response protocols.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes
World.content:
Israel's military has moved to try to stop a group of settlers from besieging three homes in the occupied West Bank. One was owned by a Palestinian American, prompting an unusually sharp rebuke from the US ambassador.

Israel has sent soldiers to try to protect three homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra that have been surrounded by a small group of Israeli settlers for several days.

One of the three homes is owned by a Palestinian American, and the incident prompted an unusually critical reponse from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically considered an ally of Israel's settler movement.

The case comes amid continued Israeli settlement building, which is considered illegal under international law, in parts of the occupied West Bank, and allegations from critics of the Israeli government that it sometimes turns a blind eye to, or does too little to prevent, settler violence against Palestinians.

What is happening and where?

Starting on Sunday, a group of settlers started gathering around three houses in the village of Qusra.

One of the buildings belongs to Palestinian-American homeowner Loui Ridi. Local officials said the settlers sometimes numbered several dozen. They supposedly threw strones, attempted to bring down a stone wall, and prevented occupants from leaving their homes as their supplies dwindled.

Israel's military moved into the area on Wednesday and moved settlers away from the properties Image: Nidal Eshtayeh/AP/dpa/picture alliance

Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida — who had holed up in the house with his son — said on Thursday morning that they had been moved to another home by the Israeli military but still could not leave the area some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Palestinian city of Nablus. Loui Ridi resides in Ohio but owns the property.

Israel's IDF military said its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" near the homes, and detained one Israeli. It wasn't immediately clear if the individual was subject to arrest or investigation, or just detention.

The local mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, said that Israeli forces evacuated seven Palestinian households from their homes to make space for soldiers to take up positions in the village. He said that the settlers remained in other parts of the village, despite being removed from their outposts.

Locals said the village was on effective lockdown.

"No one is allowed to enter. Even food and water are prohibited from reaching those besieged," the Associated Press cited Yasser Ahmad, a resident of a neighboring village, as saying as he watched the operation unfold from one hilltop over.

Qusra is in one of the most violent pockets of the northern West Bank, surrounded by settlements. Its mosque was damaged in attacks last month.

Qusra has been a frequent flashpoint of late; its mosque was set on fire in a settler attack in late July Image: Debbie Hill/UPI/newscom/picture alliance

What did US Ambassador Huckabee say about the incident?

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically a supporter of the Israeli settler movement — but also critical of settler violence — spoke out in unusually sharp terms against an incident impacting a US citizen in the West Bank.

"The actions of those doing this to this family's home is criminal," he said. "Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior."

However, Huckabee also repeatedly defended both US and Israeli authorities response to the incident, saying the US Embassy in Jerusalem had been "very involved," and that "the IDF and Israel Police have gone at our request to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this."

He later repeated this message, posting video footage seeming to show Israeli security vehicles driving into the area.

The UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory on Thursday called on the Israeli authorities to "immediately" act against the settlers .

"These criminal actions by the settlers, supported or acquiesced to by Israel, the occupying power, are making life unbearable for these Palestinian families, and are clearly aimed at forcing them to leave their homes and land," it said in a statement.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anitta Hipper called on Israel to take "concrete action to prevent settler violence."

What's the wider issue with West Bank settlement building and settler violence?

Palestinians and some in the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians, as such cases have increased in recent years since the October 7 attacks and amid the war in Gaza.

Israeli government officials tend to describe the violence as the actions of a few fringe youth acting outside the law. The UN's human rights office (OHCHR) said 18 Palestinians have died in the first seven months of this year in attacks involving settlers.

Most of the international community condemns Israeli settlement building in the West Bank as an impediment to a lasting peace and the so-called two-state solution.

More than 500,000 Israelis live — most with but also some without Israeli government authorization and support — in the West Bank, which is home to roughly 3 million Palestinians.

The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War, as part of a future state. Many settlers and some members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government claim the area should belong to Israel, often citing a mixture historical, religious and security reasons.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Russia faces further grain export cuts after port shutdowns

Russia is set to cut grain exports further this month after operations were halted at its main Black Sea and Azov Sea ports, with another major terminal suspending activity.

KSK, Russia's largest sea grain terminal, on Thursday said it had stopped operations for safety reasons, meaning all three grain terminals at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk are now out of action.

Two other Novorossiysk terminals, NZT and NKHP, were shut on Wednesday following a large Ukrainian drone attack on the port.

Sources told Reuters that NKHP's loading gallery suffered severe damage and could remain offline for months, while NZT sustained lighter damage and may reopen sooner.

Andrey Sizov, head of the Sovecon consultancy, said the shutdowns could reduce Russian grain exports by between 700,000 and 1.2 million tonnes in August alone.

He warned that markets were underestimating the risk posed by the growing escalation in the Black Sea and Azov Sea region.

World.title: How Germany's drone defense fails
World.content:
Drone defense is a priority for the German government. The latest dramatic incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport shows there are still substantial shortcomings.

How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."

Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.

Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange.

"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.

Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police

Germany has so far done little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.

Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unclear responsibilities

Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.

Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."

From printing to presses to drones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Airports, train stations still lack protection

There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.

The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Eritrea: Rising political weight along key shipping arteries
World.content:
Amid growing tensions and security risks in the Horn of Africa, Eritrea, with its strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, is emerging as an important player in the region.

Across the Horn of Africa, geopolitical interests of various countries continue to cause tensions and conflict as part of the growing competition for political influence over the region.

In its own right, the small country of Eritrea appears to be gaining in importance within this context: The autocratic state run by long-standing ruler Isaias Afwerki controls strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, especially with its ports of Assab and Massawa.

In July, a series of diplomatic consultations in Cairo involving regional powers like Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and a high-ranking US envoy highlighted Eritrea's growing role in helping to coordinate approaches to resolving serious security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and to facilitate trade.

Eritrea's unique location along this maritime route is notably becoming more and more strategic in light of international trade conflicts. The small nation's coastline near the Bab-al-Mandab Strait stretches for more than 1,000 kilometers (621.4 miles), bordering Sudan to the northwest and Djibouti to the southeast.

But Eritrea's main strategic importance relies on who is on the other side of the strait, which at its narrowest point measures less than 30 kilometers.

A small country at a strategically important location

"Yemen lies on the other side of the Red Sea, which makes Eritrea's location particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk," Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration (CRI) in London, told DW.

"The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns."

Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki has been ruling the country since its independence in 1993 as a strict one-party authoritarian regime Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance

The Houthi militia, propped up by Iran, have been attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea from the Yemeni coastline.

For the past ten years, Yemen has also been witnessing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in its midst: Ongoing violence, economic collapse, droughts and floods have exacerbated the suffering in the country, according to a report published by the UN Refugee Agency last month.

Sayed meanwhile emphasizes that in Eritrea, the strong dictatorship entrenched for decades does not tolerate any type of dissent. In many international freedom indexes, the African nation often only comes second to North Korea.

Since the country was officially founded 32 years ago, there have been no elections in the one-party state under long-time ruler Afwerki.

A unique sense of stability — for now

But this is also exactly why there are no violent conflicts in the country. Compared to other players in the broader region like Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen, Eritrea appears to be an island of peace where it is easy to do business.

"For this reason, all countries — including regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which controls the Suez Canal — want to maintain stable relations with Eritrea," Sayed highlights.

At the same time, this could eventually prove to be the country's Achilles' heel: "The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions. That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power," says Sayed.

There is no strong figure in the 80-year-old autocrat's inner circle seen as a clear successor. This has raised some concern that the security situation could collapse once the president might no longer be in power, according to Sayed.

This sailor from Yemen's internationally recognized government is in charge of controlling activity on the Red Sea Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Alternative to the Strait of Hormuz

Still, Eritrea continues to exert its influence as the Red Sea has emerged a crucial sea route for the world, and especially for the Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, according to Sayed.

The war with Iran has further reinforced the nation's position, as this crisis has once again shown the central geopolitical importance of maritime chokepoints such as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.

One viable alternative, should the Strait of Hormuz remain repeatedly blocked, would be for these Gulf nations and their partners to find routes via Saudi ports located further up on the Red Sea.

While the Saudis have pipelines running from some of the interior regions of the country from where oil is extracted and produced to the port of Yanbu-Al-Bahr on the Red Sea, this alternative route could easily be compromised when it comes to security, potentially driving up oil prices even higher than what they currently are.

"For this reason, Eritrea today is of great strategic importance. This has been the case for centuries and will continue to be the case," Sayed emphasizes.

Why Ethiopia seeks control over Assab port To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopia demands direct Red Sea access

Meanwhile, Eritrea's neighbors, particularly landlocked Ethiopia, are fighting hard to maintain access to the Red Sea as a trade route, Sayed adds, in particular for oil exports from the Horn of Africa to the rest of the world, especially to Europe and the Americas.

For decades, Djibouti has dominated regional trade logistics as Ethiopia's most important seaport partner, while Eritrea has been sidelined economically.

But Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has for years been demanding sovereign access to the sea — more than three decades after the country's split with Eritrea: when Eritrea gained its independence in 1993, Ethiopia lost its direct access, and has since been relying on its neighbors for all its sea trade.

However, maintaining a sense of neutrality and balance is proving to be a walk on a tightrope: Earlier in 2026, the fragile relations with between Ethiopia and Eritrea's Asmara region had already threatened to escalate amid a dispute over Ethiopia's access to the maritime trade route.

Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The key context for Eritrea's recent strategic maneuvers in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea is the escalating tensions with Ethiopia," says Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council.

"Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa. Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates' armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the US should be viewed against this backdrop," he tells DW.

Meanwhile, a new trade corridor on the Red Sea is also taking shape: In May 2026, Eritrea and Egypt signed an agreement to establish direct freight connections between Egyptian and Eritrean ports on the Red Sea to expand independent trade and supply chains in the region.

A grave record of human rights violations

Still, there are no long-term guarantees with Eritrea, since the country's short history is almost entirely marked by violence, resulting in many people seeking a better life elsewhere.

"The first people fled Eritrea for Sudan in 1967 to escape [former Ethiopian ruler] Haile Selassie's imperial army. In the 1980s, people fled in large numbers from the Ethiopian military dictatorship. Since 2001, people have once again been fleeing in large numbers from human rights violations, military service, war, and a lack of prospects," says Magnus Treiber, a migration researcher specializing in the Horn of Africa at the Institute of Ethnology at the University of Munich.

"The causes of flight have hardly changed. However, since the European Union now offers virtually no opportunities to seek asylum, Eritreans are now fleeing all over the world."

Displacement is rife around the Horn of Africa, where various conflicts repeatedly force entire populations to seek safety elsewhere Image: GIULIA PARAVICINI/REUTERS

At least 700,000 people have left the country since its founding, which is about a fifth of its total population. The country's population growth, meanwhile, is under 2% — a low number compared to many countries in the region.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: What would a North Korean troop surge mean for Ukraine war?
World.content:
Ukraine is claiming that North Korea is preparing to send tens of thousands more troops to Russia, where they'll gain valuable battlefield experience.

North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine, with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

In late July, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict.

In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia.

North Korea has suffered thousands of casualties in the Ukraine war

Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later. Analysts believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region.

Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded.

This image, published by Ukrainian officials, shows North Korean soldiers being fitted for Russian uniforms Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front.

Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality'

South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer.

Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country.

"I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment.

"Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military."

Will North Koreans watch Russians' back?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution.

"Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW.

"North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han.

"Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine."

Russian officials praise North Koreans

"North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said.

North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean casualties, some 2,000 may have been killed.

"Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment," Han said.

"North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery."

North Korean women also moving to Russia

Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops."

"North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979.

"If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added.

Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel."

Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military

According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military."

"However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn.

"A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden."

World.title: Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive
World.content:
Rail traffic was suspended in a region of Bavaria and authorities evacuated buildings around a train station after a suspicious object was found on the tracks. Police later confirmed it did not contain explosives.

Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution on Thursday after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives.

Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene.

A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.

Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations.

A federal police bomb disposal team is examining the object Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance

Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.

Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes.
