Exclusive NationalIllness The discovery that could turn mosquito bites into vaccine booster shots Angus Dalton August 14, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After decades of research and a stroke of luck, Australian researchers have developed a new vaccination method for a disease that has dogged humanity for millennia and continues to take at least 610,000 – and counting – lives each year. The scientists hope the experimental malaria vaccine, successfully tested on mice, could transform mosquito bites into “booster shots” that fortify the body’s immune defences against the disease instead of causing infection. Associate Professor Justin Boddey, a malaria researcher at WEHI, and his colleagues may have found a way to turn mosquito bites from a disease-causing tragedy to an immune-boosting triumph. Jason South Malaria is caused by a cunning parasite that has evolved resistance to every major drug designed to treat it. Current vaccines are only 40 to 75 per cent effective, require multiple doses and often suffer from fast-waning immunity. In response to the crisis, scientists at Melbourne research institute WEHI and their collaborators have fashioned an experimental drug into a kind of chemical vaccine that allows the malaria parasite to grow within the body before killing it right before it causes disease.



That allows the body to build up key antibodies and immune cells ready to pounce on future infection. “You could think of it as using a drug to convert mosquito bites that spread malaria into vaccination events,” Associate Professor Justin Boddey, corresponding author of the new research published in the major journal Science and a laboratory head at WEHI, said. Current malaria vaccines are usually less than 90 per cent effective and need multiple doses, which is not ideal in the poverty-stricken areas where malaria is most deadly. This photo is of another trial vaccine in Kenya. AP Malaria begins when a mosquito bites someone and injects sporozoites, the infectious stage of the parasite, from its salivary glands. The sporozoites wriggle through the blood and into the liver, where they invade cells and rapidly divide. At this stage, a patient has no symptoms, but after about a week, the parasites burst from infected liver cells as “merozoites” and flood into the bloodstream, infecting and bursting red blood cells.



This marks the symptomatic stage of the infection, when the parasite begins to inflict terrible fevers, headaches, vomiting and possibly death. Killing the parasite at the late-liver stage – right before it starts sickening a patient – is the “immunogenic sweet spot”, Boddey said. Illustration of liver cells (pink) infected with a malaria parasite (green). Malaria lurks and multiplies in the liver before attacking red blood cells. Drew Berry/wehi.tv “What we’ve really happened upon here is the remarkable ability of this drug to permit sporozoite infection and liver stage development all the way through to the late liver stage, and then the drug blocks the parasites from being able to get out and invade red blood cells,” he said. The huge number of dead parasite cells then prime the body’s lasting immune response. “These large, fat, juicy liver-stage parasites are not causing any disease, but are full of antigens”, which trigger antibodies, Boddey said.



The promise behind the method is that every time someone is bitten, dead parasite cells would build up again, giving the body a chance to re-fortify its immune response. In mice, the treatment generated anti-malarial antibodies and T cells, which learn to recognise the parasite and “execute” infected cells, even after the drug left the body. Mice given the vaccine and infected with the rodent version of malaria didn’t get sick and, when bitten by 10 malarial mosquitoes almost two years later, retained their immunity. Using bioengineered mice grafted with human liver cells, the researchers were able to test their treatment on the strain of malaria that infects humans, and showed it also successfully killed the human-adapted version of the parasite. “Mice have been quite predictive in previous malaria vaccine studies,” Boddey said. “So we’re very excited about the possibility that this will work in people, and we’re ready to start doing clinical trials in this space very, very soon.”



Boddey and two of his colleagues have submitted patents related to the vaccination method. Related Article AI The device detecting the world’s deadliest creature A major paper in 2017 revealed two malaria proteins called plasmepsin IX and X are essential for malaria to escape liver cells and get into the bloodstream. Boddey and his colleagues at WEHI and pharmaceutical company MSD had already been working on trying to disrupt a different protein, which didn’t work. But it turned out the drug could disrupt plasmepsin IX and X. That’s the discovery that allowed the scientists to turn liver cells from a parasite nursery into a death trap.



“It’s a bit of a dream come true, and it’s a huge team effort,” Boddey said. “Chance favours the prepared.” Malaria researcher Dr Claire Sayers, a molecular biologist at the University of NSW who wasn’t involved in the study, said the new research addressed the major challenge of both stopping malaria and building long-term immunity. “This is an exciting preclinical study that presents an innovative approach to tackling malaria and showcases the value of discovery science,” she said. “The critical next step will be to see whether this promising approach can translate into meaningful protection in people under real-world conditions of malaria exposure.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Andrew Brooks Why has the quiz changed?



Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? You can find a running tally in green at the top right of the quiz. Can I see all the quiz questions at a glance? No, we challenge players to complete the quiz one question at a time. Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. World.title: Demon adds to fairytale comeback, leads her side to glory in her first match in 355 days
World.content:
Melbourne midfielder Olivia Purcell delivered a serious reminder of both her talent and importance to the Demons’ line-up with a best-on-ground showing against the Hawks on Thursday night in her first AFLW game in almost 12 months.

Purcell went down with a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament in round two last season and worked tirelessly to get back in time for this year’s season opener for the Dees. She finished the clash with 32 disposals, nine tackles and 354 metres gained as Melbourne overcame a spirited Hawthorn by 19 points, 9.6 (60) to 6.5 (41).

Mia Austin and Olivia Purcell share a moment in the Demons’ win over Hawthorn. AFL Photos

New Demons coach Tom Wilson was quick to point out what the premiership-winning midfielder meant to his side in their 19-point win.

“It speaks to her ability and the work she has put in place,” Wilson said.

World.title: Chillin’ in the City of Gold
World.content:
Ken Arnold of Leura can back up Rhoda Silber’s remark about the incongruous snow situation in Johannesburg (C8). “I can recall what was probably the same occurrence, around September 1981. A colleague in Johannesburg decided that, being the dry season, it was the ideal time renovate their roof. The day after removing the roof, it didn’t rain – it snowed.”

Going by the experience of David Fletcher of Pymble, it had happened before: “My first sighting of snow was in Joburg in August 1962 as a 4-year-old. My first snowman didn’t last too long as the snow melted by lunchtime!”

Paul Jameson of Suffolk Park writes: “My first sight of snow was when I was 8 (70 years ago) and living in the foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. That magnificent mountain always had its snow cap but unfortunately, it was not fashionable to climb it. I was back there last year and saw very little snow left, another effect of climate change. I’m now too old to climb Kilimanjaro.”

“While staying in Dirranbandi, Queensland, we were approached with a question from other travellers from Brisbane about the ‘white stuff’ on the side of the road,” recalls Janice Creenaune of Austinmer. “‘Cotton’ we replied. They’d thought it might be snow but were in too big of a ‘rig’ to stop and investigate on the one-lane roads.”

“Silent Movie (C8), Mel Brooks at his best (C8),” remarks Brett Jack of Bonnyrigg Heights. “An all-star movie with only one word of dialogue in the entire film - ‘Non!’, and that word uttered by none other than mime maestro Marcel Marceau. Brilliant!” Serge Nemaz of Illawong agrees and hopes Herman Beyersdorf forked out for the headphones: “Definitely worth the $2, I would think!”

World.title: ‘Weaker at home’: Wong’s veiled warning to One Nation on national security
World.content:
PoliticsFederalForeign relations ‘Weaker at home’: Wong’s veiled warning to One Nation on national security Natassia Chrysanthos August 13, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Foreign Minister Penny Wong will paint Pauline Hanson’s call for a monoculture as a major threat to national security, making the case that Australia’s diversity is a bulwark against global instability while reaffirming that regional diplomacy is Labor’s top priority. Wong will argue that her own Malaysian background demonstrates how migrants have enriched Australia and helped it find common ground with other people in the world, also pointing to Burundi refugee Nestory Irankunda and his opening goal of the Socceroos’ recent World Cup campaign. Foreign Minister Penny Wong listens to an address at the National Press Club last month. Dominic Lorrimer Her speech comes after a charged debate over multiculturalism was spawned in June by Hanson saying Australia should be monocultural. The One Nation leader later backtracked, saying the diverse Socceroos football team was an example of what she was talking about. Labor has since worn multiculturalism as a badge of pride as it seeks to counter Hanson’s surging popularity, and Wong’s speech will take this a step further by making the direct link between diversity and successful foreign policy.



“Our multicultural society, along with our economy and our democratic institutions, are essential elements of our resilience and raise the costs for those who seek to coerce us,” Wong will say in a speech to the Lowy Institute on Friday. Related Article Protests ‘We are not stupid kids’: Perth students rally against Pauline Hanson “And those who seek to divide us for clicks and votes should know that they make us weaker at home and more vulnerable in the world.” Wong will argue this is increasingly important given rising global instability, with China’s military buildup and recent ballistic missile tests in the Pacific, and United States President Donald Trump’s war with Iran. She will say Australia’s multicultural make-up gives it particular currency in the Indo-Pacific region, since more than a million Australians trace their families to South-East Asia, and more still to South and North Asia.



“No other country I have visited can meet this region so naturally on its own terms,” Wong will say. “We are more prosperous because of our diversity. We have more choices because of it. We are more capable in the world, and we are more able to find common ground with so many of the world’s peoples because of it.” The Albanese government has re-oriented Australian foreign policy since coming to power, focusing on regional relationships in South-East Asia and the Pacific while building alliances outside the United States to shore up its strategic influence as a middle power. Australian foreign policy has historically centred on the US alliance, regional engagement and a rules-based order, but Wong last year shifted this formula to put the region first and add another pillar of “resilience” to Australia’s diplomatic priorities. Expanding on this approach on Friday, Wong will say: “The first priority must be the region, because this is where Australia has the most on the line.



“The second priority is relationships. It is not enough to exclusively champion the alliance. Our priority since coming to government has been to diversify our relationships, while strengthening traditional partnerships with the United Kingdom and the United States. Related Article Foreign relations Japanese ambassador moves to quash melon drama, defend Albanese “We have always understood that President Trump envisages a different role for the United States in the world. Even so, the United States remains the world’s largest economic and military power, with daily influence over international events that have consequences for Australia.” Wong will point to Australia’s ability to secure fuel and supplies from Asian neighbours when the Strait of Hormuz was closed due to the US-Iran war earlier this year as evidence this strategy had been successful. She will also reference a range of pacts recently signed with Indonesia, Timor-Leste, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu, Tuvalu and Nauru to argue Australia had made “transformational breakthroughs” in building regional security.



“These agreements help us contribute to a strategic balance of power in our region ... Those relationships must be reinforced, thoughtfully, deliberately and continuously, by every part of government, businesses and the community. Security is everyone’s responsibility,” she will say. But these would be undermined by talking down the region or retreating from global institutions, Wong will say, in a thinly veiled reference to Hanson. “The ability of Australians to connect with people from every part of the world is a national asset,” she will say. “The call for a monoculture is a call for Australia to curtail our choices and cut off our connections … To look inwards, to have no friends to work with, no partners to trade with, no opportunities to grow from. To be lonely in a dangerous world.” Wong will warn that damage to the country will be done “well before we could ever realise this melancholic fantasy of monoculture”.



“Because Australians would be turned against each other. Australia would be a more hostile place,” she will say. “At a time where external and internal forces are seeking to divide us, turning Australians against each other makes us more vulnerable. Division makes us easier to exploit, it doesn’t make us stronger. Turning Australians against each other is the opposite of patriotism. “Our resilience starts with how we choose to live together... It starts with respecting that multicultural Australia is the only Australia that has ever existed.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Nelson voters provide Christopher Luxon with a welcome respite
World.content:
The political drama of Christopher Luxon's leadership challenge has been ignored by National party supporters in Nelson at a public meeting on Thursday night.

Around 600 people turned up to the meeting at Annesbrook Events Centre, where the prime minister fielded questions about employment, housing affordability, crime and sustainability among other issues.

Luxon entered the room to loud cheering and applause, his first public meeting since surviving a confidence vote following an urgent caucus meeting on Wednesday.

He was joined by Nelson candidate Blair Cameron and West Coast Tasman candidate Katie Milne and told the crowd he enjoyed "getting out of the bubble of Wellington" and hearing "the good, the bad and the ugly" from people.

During the hour-long meeting there were no references to the recent confidence vote or questions from the crowd about Luxon's leadership, but instead a focus on the party's plan to "fix the basics" and "build the future".

The recent rumblings within National were not mentioned during the public meeting. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Early on in the meeting when a National Party sign bearing that slogan on the lectern came unstuck, Luxon grabbed before it fell and said, "actually, I was going to fix some basics and build the future right now".

He fielded questions on what National would do to help young New Zealanders, how the new India free trade agreement would help small and struggling businesses, why the environmental issues facing the country weren't being taken more seriously, how homelessness was being addressed and how National planned to tackle youth crime and violence in the community.

High school student Noah Johnson told Luxon young people were facing major uncertainty around housing, education, and employment and asked how National would address that if re-elected.

Luxon said the reason he got into politics was to rebuild the proposition for young people in New Zealand.

"In the last 12 months we had a 14 per cent growth in Kiwis leaving Australia and coming home to New Zealand, which is really exciting and really encouraging."

RNZ / Samantha Gee

He said National was focused on building a more economically productive economy, addressing housing supply issues by reducing bureacracy and had a policy to make KiwiSaver compulsory to help people build retirement savings.

"We've started that work, we've got more to do, but I'd be pretty excited as a young person that this could be a great place to build a family and to live your life here."

The final question of the night came from a deaf, former sex worker who said the loss of thousands of public sector jobs meant her business in Wellington collapsed overnight.

Through an interpreter, she told Luxon there were many self-employed people in the sex industry and it provided reliable work, but National's economic policies had made it difficult to work in the industry and many sex workers had gone on the benefit or were working two jobs to survive.

Luxon said the issue was a "demand problem" and that National was focused on economic growth and creating new opportunities for people.

"We're also focused on getting more efficiency in our public service and we are going to restructure it and reform it. We want it to be less bureaucratic and we want it to be delivering better for New Zealanders and offering better service."

After the meeting, Luxon spent almost as much time as he had onstage speaking to people who queued up to see him. He said a lot had offered words of encouragement.

He acknowledged it had been a tough 48 hours in the leadup to the caucus meeting in Wellington.

"We came out of a room very united, very determined that we are going to work to make this election about a very clear choice."

National had a responsible economic plan, focused on long term growth, Luxon said.

World.title: PNG rugby worry about league impact, amid ongoing suspension
World.content:
Papua New Guinea Rugby is worried more union players might be lured to rugby league, as it continues to be suspended by World Rugby.

The interim president of the PNG Rugby Union, Vince Karawa, told RNZ Pacific from Port Moresby that the Australian government's large financial investments in rugby league in PNG has already seen players moving to the 13-man code.

The Australian government has approved AUD$600 million over 10 years to support rugby league in the Pacific, including PNG.

At the same time the Australians also budgeted AUD$190 million for the establishment of the PNG Chiefs franchise team that will make its debut in the NRL in 2028.

Overshadowed by league in PNG, Karawa fears more young people and current players will leave union if their suspension is prolonged.

He has called on Oceania Rugby to come to the table, sit and genuinely discuss a way forward, especially in their demand for grants given to the union to be reimbursed.

"Currently the games are still on and quite active at the moment," he said.

"The question everyone is asking is, when will the the suspension be uplifted?

"The game's being jeopardised through the suspension.

"Rugby players have been lured to rugby league, so that's that's something that we've raised to Oceania Rugby, saying to them the more the suspension is prolonged we are on the verge of losing good players to rugby league."

Karawa said they are still waiting on Oceania Rugby to open the door for a round-the-table discussion "for us to really sit down and discuss all these issues surrounding rugby and PNG".

Roadmap

Oceania Rugby delivered the suspension notice to the PNGRU in 2024 over breaches of its tournament obligations, governance and financial non-compliance.

Oceania Rugby commissioned an independent inquiry and established an Independent Judicial Panel to review PNGRU's finances and governance in the months that followed.

Oceania Rugby general manager Frank Puletua said the ball is in PNGRU's court.

"We've been in regular contact with PNGRU and World Rugby throughout this process," he said.

"There's a roadmap agreed by all parties, and we want to see PNGRU back in good standing as soon as they meet what's required."

Karawa acknowleged the contact made by Oceania Rugby but insists they need to have face-to-face discussions to iron out the issues.

Karawa said they have met "most of the sanctions that were placed by Oceania Rugby" and the union has been working with the regional body.

He revealed the current board is a new one, with members elected after the suspension in 2024.

He said the main area they are working on now is clearing a debt that is puzzling them.

That is because around AUD$130,000 in grants given to the union between 2018 to 2023 is now one of the main issues that is affecting their reinstatement.

Oceania Rugby is saying PNGRU needs to repay the grant.

General manager Puletua said last week repaying that debt is critical for PNG Rugby's reinstatment.

"Reinstatement depends on PNGRU clearing a longstanding debt and meeting governance conditions set out in the roadmap," he said

"Some details of the process will stay confidential given the sensitivities for people and organisations in PNG."

But Karawa said their understanding is that they need to send in acquittals for grants extended to PNG, and not to repay the money as it was never a loan.

"So, as far as we understand, this grants are supposed to assist organisations in terms of setting up programmes and developing rugby programmes, assisting all the unions," he said.

"The grants were used to assist the international events, especially rugby tournaments where the national teams competed in.

"They're asking that those funds to be reimbursed. As far as we understand you have to acquit for those funds."

On the defensive: PNG's women's team fend off Tonga. Oceania Rugby

Karawa said "in terms of reimbursing, that's something that we need to really discuss with Oceania Rugby".

The financial assistance was given to PNGRU under the old board but since the new board were elected the burden of payment has fallen on them, Karawa said.

He said getting Oceania Rugby to meet them and agree on a payment plan agreement going forward so they can be reinstated is what they are asking for.

"We have programmes running in schools, we have development pathway programmes going forward and we need exposure to regional and international events.

"This can't happen because we're still suspended."

Work-ons

Karawa said PNG Rugby is reaching out to stakeholders and will keep trying to get Oceania Rugby to sit with them.

Regarding governnance and management, he said they have worked with their local member unions on ensuring that they follow the World Rugby guidelines and are transparent.

"We have worked with them to understand the systems, the process and they need to meet the requirements like you know, the reportings and financial reports and executive reports," he said.

"Our focus has been on making sure they stop the usual systems they had operated in maybe in the past."

"The whole purpose is to make sure that the rugby administration and operation and done correctly going forward and we want to set a precedent so that the next board executives don't fall short."

World.title: 'Voter suppression by stealth' - NZ govt accused of locking out Pasifika vote
World.content:
The Minister for Pacific Peoples has denied that a recent law change ruling out late enrolment will disenfranchise Pasifika voters.

However, others beg to differ, echoing a report from the government's own Attorney-General at the time this change and other voter restictions were announced.

The change means that in the upcoming November general election, voters have to enrol 13 days before election day, after the government ended the ability for eligible voters to enrol and cast special votes during the voting period.

In the report, former Attorney-General Judith Collins acknowledged that special votes were more likely to come from areas with larger Māori, Asian and Pasifika communities, and that younger people are more likely to cast special votes.

Despite this, the Justice and Pacific Peoples' Minister Paul Goldsmith said he didn't accept that the change would disenfranchise Pacific voters.

"Everybody is required by the legislation to get enrolled. We don't think New Zealanders are less capable than Australians, and if Australians can get it done 30 days before the election, we're confident that New Zealanders can get it done in a timely fashion as well," he told RNZ Pacific.

Green Party MP Teanau Tuiono talks with Samoan counterparts during an inter-parliamentary trip to Apia, 11 July 2023. Johnny Blades / VNP

But Green Party MP Teanau Tuiono said the government was making democracy harder to access.

"Election day enrolment has allowed thousands of people to participate who might otherwise have missed out," he said.

"Taking that option away will disproportionately affect communities that already face barriers to engagement, and in particular our Pasifika communities."

Special votes counted during the 2023 general election included over 97,000 people who registered for the first time during the voting period.

However, Goldsmith said he had "every confidence" that people who are entitled to vote will have every opportunity to do so.

"So my message to them right here right now is: it's not hard," said Goldsmith.

Efficiency excuse 'a lot of rot'

New Zealand has a highly trusted and transparent electoral system, yet the government is arguing it is making the democratic system more efficient by removing the ability of a sizeable chunk of voters to participate in the system.

Tuiono said special votes made up nearly a third of ballots in largely Pasifika electorates and described the government's claim about improving efficiency as an excuse.

"I think that's a lot of rot, that actually what this is is voter suppression by stealth," he told RNZ Pacific.

"Every eligible New Zealander should be able to vote, regardless of how busy their lives are or how often they move. So these changes are literally locking people out of decisions that govern their lives."

Winston Peters' NZ First Party has a new electoral policy that could also curb the Pacific vote. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Permanent residents in NZ First's crosshairs

Meanwhile, other members of the governing coalition are campaigning on introducing new electoral policy that could further squeeze out the Pasifika vote.

NZ First has announced a policy where only New Zealand citizens have the right to vote for central and local government elections and referenda.

Paul Goldsmith said the National Party hadn't yet come out in support of it, adding that it hadn't yet had a full caucus discussion about it.

But Tuiono said the policy was terrible and unfairly targets people.

World.title: US and several Pacific countries hit out at Chinese nuclear missile test, after PIF misses chance
World.content:
A number of Pacific Islands countries have joined the United States in effectively accusing China of skirting the rules after Beijing's recent nuclear-capable missile test in the Pacific.

A joint statement released by the US government on August 11th implicitly claimed that China gave the world less than 24 hours notice before launching a dummy warhead in South Pacific waters, near Tuvalu, in early July.

The statement had four Pacific Islands Forum country signatures, including New Zealand, Australia, and two island states which both recognise Taiwan over China - the Marshall Islands and Palau.

It comes just days after a PIF Foreign Ministers meeting last week in Suva failed to produce a joint statement condeming China's nuclear missle test.

In the statement, the US and dozens of other countries said that "recent missile testing in the Pacific area" fell short of standard practices that most states use to avoid the appearance of an attack - and prevent a miscalculated strike-back.

"Conducting nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests without sufficient advance notice and detail is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests.

"We remain committed to working with all countries to strengthen the implementation of and expand notification frameworks and to hold accountable any state whose actions fall short of its responsibilities."

Starboard Maritime Intelligence

Was there enough warning?

The exact amount of warning time China gave to Pacific countries remains an open question. Beijing insists that it followed international law.

New Zealand for one stated that the test happened "within hours" of China's warning, echoed by Australia, Japan and Papua New Guinea.

A US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency issued a HYDROPAC navigational safety warning at 5:50am UTC on July 5th, around the area where the missile would finally land - at 12:01pm on July 6th, more than 30 hours later.

Starboard Maritime Intelligence analyst Mark Douglas said that such area warnings aren't the same as forewarning a ballistic missile test - a navigational safety warnings are triggered by a range of activities, including satellite launches that don't have the same geopolitical impact.

But he also said that, evidenced by the positioning of three Yuan Wang-class tracking ships, one of which was in Suva, the test had been planned for some time.

"It's been widely reported that China provided limited notice to Pacific nations of the test - by which time China had prepared two possible launch options, and placed ships along the flight routes."

All the same, Douglas said that the advanced notice that countries did have was unlikely to inspire trust in China.

"These actions... will likely result in the closer monitoring of Chinese vessels, and particularly satellite tracking vessels, in the Pacific."

Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Ministers Meeting 2026 was held at the PIF Secretariat in Suva. 7 August 2026 RNZ Pacific / Susana Suisuiki

Statement of influence

The majority of countries in the Pacific Islands Forum have voiced concern about missile testing in the Pacific, which is a nuclear-free zone.

But while some countries had been reluctant to single out China for its test, most countries were pushing for a joint statement on the issue at last week's Suva meeting of regional foreign ministers.

It's understood Nauru and Kiribati, both closely aligned with China, stood in the way of full consensus on a statement.

An outcomes document released by PIF downplayed this, saying that Ministers "recognised and reaffirmed the value of a consensus-based regional statement" - requesting that officials wrangle something together by the end of the month.

But a frustrated New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters accused Nauru and Kiribati of gaming the system, as a way of showing support to "an external partner."

"They were seeking to use the need for consensus as actually a veto provision, look at it that way," he told reporters on Saturday.

In contrast, PIF Secretary-General Baron Waqa said that it was simply a case of finding the right formatting, and that they were "committed" to getting there in the end.

"There are other ideas that it should be a general statement covering any tests in the Pacific," Waqa insisted.

The Chinese embassy in New Zealand - perhaps incensed after Peters' told a Chinese MP to go back to his home country - lashed out on August 12th, stating Peters has "humiliated himself" in Suva.

"The outcome delivered Peters a resounding slap in the face. Pacific Island countries clearly showed little interest in the agenda he promoted," it read.

It went further, accusing New Zealand of a power grab, and an attempt to become the Pacific's "regional decision maker."

"Peters' failure to achieve his goal fully demonstrates that Pacific Island nations do not want to be used as pawns by others."

World.title: 'Local tourism dividend': ACT Party proposes bed tax alternative
World.content:
The ACT Party has come up with a bed tax alternative: giving councils $1 for every guest night in their area, funded from GST and existing visitor levies.

Leader David Seymour said ACT would campaign on a "local tourism dividend".

He believed it was a smarter option than a bed tax, which would charge guests a small percentage on top of their short term hotels and B&B stays.

Seymour estimated the dividend would give councils more than $40 million annually, based on 2026 guest night figures.

"The reality is that tourists already pay a lot more GST than they take out of New Zealand in services," Seymour said.

"The problem is they pay it to the central government rather than the councils who bear most of the cost."

The policy fixed a problem all councils faced without adding hotel bill charges or expanding government, he said.

A bed tax has been floated as an answer to councils struggling to pay for often long overdue infrastructure upgrades.

National leader Christopher Luxon on Monday told RNZ his party may explore one if it's re-elected, but Seymour immediately poured cold water on the idea.

The dividend would not raise the cost of staying in New Zealand, reduce the revenue of accommodation providers, or add any compliance burden, he said.

"The principle is: no new workers at IRD administering a new tax, no new filing for New Zealand businesses, just a straight transfer once a year from government to council based on the number of bed nights, which we already have statistics for."

Seymour said the system could begin as early as 1 July next year, while a new tax would take at least a year longer because it would require legislation.

World.title: Glitchy apps, deal disparity: Here's what's upsetting customers
World.content:
Lots of New Zealanders say companies aren't meeting their expectations, and they're upset about new customers getting better deals than existing ones.

A survey by Accenture Song measured the gap between what brands promised and the reality that customers experienced. It showed 69 percent of people said companies were falling short.

The greatest gap was in media and entertainment, followed by groceries, then the utilities sector and telcos, general insurance and banking.

New Zealand lead Storm Day said loyalty tax was a particular gripe. She said across banks, power companies and telcos, people were upset about seeing new customers offered better deals than existing customers.

"One of the biggest themes that came through was this idea of loyalty tax... people are seeing new customers getting way better treatment, way better deals and people are just frustrated and over it.

"I think that is also a real opportunity for brands…if you can identify and demonstrate value, and even in your messaging to your loyal customers, I think that that is a real opportunity to win them over and win back trust and make sure people are choosing your brand over another, especially with agentic AI, you can almost make switching so much easier."

People were also wondering whether their bills were deliberately hard to decode, and whether specials were as good as they appeared to be.

In the utilities sector, people were upset about new apps that were not an improvement on the old one, and only being contacted when prices were increasing.

"In the utilities sector specifically there's been a whole heap of disruption, also with AI as well it makes it easier for customers to decode complex policies and things and now they can do that I think they're also really voicing why brands haven't ever stepped in. There's a feeling that policies are almost impossible to decode and pricing structures are really impossible to compare. There's little differentiation in that category specifically. People are really frustrated."

Day said increasing use of AI was helping people to identify when they were not getting a good deal.

"Consumers are already using AI to compare prices, decode policies, translate jargon, and hunt better deals. They're increasingly expecting brands to proactively do this for them, with clear communication and greater transparency.

"The brands closing the gap and winning are the ones using technology like AI to simplify the customer experience, while keeping the experience human-led. That's how they build trust, deepen loyalty, and drive long-term growth."

New Zealanders are loyal when it comes to electricity providers. Boris Zhitkov

Consumer NZ spokesperson Jessica Walker said the research echoed some of the themes Consumer has found in its surveying. She said there had been a big dip in trust across all sectors in April but that had rebounded.

Its most recent update found that customer satisfaction was improving in most sectors, except energy.

She said the idea of a loyalty tax was something that she saw upsetting people too.

"There's a lot of people that assume they are being looked after by a provider.

"We know that especially when it comes to electricity people tend to stick. They presume that the retailer they're with is going to be giving them the best possible price. In fact at our last count we found 38 percent of people think all electricity providers charge the same.

"That's just not true, the average saving on Powerswitch at the moment is about $470 a year. So there definitely is money to be saved by switching. But then it seems that New Zealanders are a really loyal bunch. So there's this assumption that your retailer is looking after you, but then when you find out that that's not the case then that leads to upset."

She said people were often shocked that they could save money but also hurt that their loyalty was not rewarded.

Glitchy apps are a particular source of frustration for customers across the country. Photo by Vardan Papikyan on Unsplash

"In fact worse than unrewarded, they're being taxed. They're paying a penalty."

Walker said people could also be caught out by bundled deals, where one household had multiple services with the same provider.

Consumer research indicated that people who bundled services tended to get tied in with their provider because it felt more complicated to switch.

"For a year, you might be getting a good deal. But if you stick, you could be paying over the odds for all the utilities that you've bundled together. And it's also another barrier to switching, psychological … it's all bundled together and it just feels like too much hassle. So it's something that we urge caution on.

"If you are going to sign up to a bundle, look how long the fixed term is and then just do double check if you're able to switch. You can probably make savings off the back of your fixed term as well."

World.title: Flu-related hospitalisations in Auckland double in space of a week
World.content:
Flu-related hospitalisations in Auckland have doubled in the space of a week, as the country's flu season begins to bite slightly later than usual.

Dr Hannah Cooper, a public health physician in the health intelligence team at PHF Science, said in recent weeks - particularly the past seven days - cases have climbed sharply.

"In the past week [there's been] an increase in flu-related hospitalisations in the Auckland region. They actually doubled in the previous week compared to the week prior."

However, they were still within the normal range for peak season seen in previous years.

For the week ending 9 August, the rate was 3.781 per 100,000 people - up from 1.574 the week before.

Flu cases among hospital admissions with respiratory symptoms. PHF Science

"Flu, particularly in cold weather, spreads more easily," Cooper said.

The cold snap had seen more people spending their time indoors, spreading the virus more effectively.

Last year's season was late too, which had pushed the 2026 season later in the year, with people retaining some immunity from last year's infections.

Public awareness of the different strains was also on the rise.

"Now that you can do a test from the pharmacy to see what kind of cold or flu virus you have… that's really raising awareness about flu activity," said Cooper.

Despite the spike in cases, the vaccine was proving effective, according to their data.

"The really good news is that the flu viruses that are circulating this season are a very good match. The vaccine is a very good match for those viruses."

It wasn't too late to get the vaccine, she said.

Emergency departments (EDs) and services around the country are also feeling the strain.

St John declared a "major incident" last week, after a "highly unusual" sudden spike in demand correlated with the recent cold snap, and an influx in people requesting ambulances for winter illnesses such as influenza and respiratory issues.

EDs remained over capacity in many areas - Wellington had its busiest day in more than a year earlier this week.

Nurses Organisation delegate Ryan O'Connell, who works in the Wellington ED, said: "For about three or four days in a row, we were getting over 200 patients per 24-hour period. Anything over 200 is usually quite high for the ED."

It was "harsh on morale", he said. "You've just got this waiting room filling up with people you triaged hours ago and wish were at least lying down on a trolley at this point."

"There's so many people to look after and not enough staff and not enough room to look after these people. But you make do anyway and you try your best."

Pressure on GPs was meaning appointments were scarce, which left people turning to EDs when their condition worsened.

"I constantly see patients and triage patients who say, 'I was trying to get a GP appointment… maybe I couldn't get one this week, and I'm just not coping with this at home.'"

With the main centres slammed, he felt for those in the more rural parts of the country.

World.title: Gisborne residents urged to be ready for flooding and slips
World.content:
Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is urging residents to be ready for potential surface flooding, slips and more as heavy rain moves in.

An orange heavy rain warning is in effect for Gisborne/Tai Rāwhiti, north of Tolaga Bay, until 8pm on Friday night.

Between 90 and 120mm of rain is expected, with potential peak rates of up to 20mm per hour.

The public are being told to clear gutters and drains, steer clear of low-lying areas while the heaviest rain comes through, and drive to the conditions.

A heavy rain watch is also in effect for Bay of Plenty, in and around Kawerau. Periods of heavy rain are possible through to 9am on Friday.

"Amounts may approach warning criteria with localised downpours possible," MetService said on Thursday night.

World.title: Roosters force first NRL lead change in five months
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have moved to the top of the NRL ladder for the first time in five years, leapfrogging Penrith with a 12-6 win over the Panthers.

With three rounds remaining, the Roosters are in the box seat to win the minor premiership thanks to a two-try showing from Daly Cherry-Evans and an electrifying performance from his halves partner Sam Walker at Parramatta Stadium on Thursday night.

Walker this week parked contract extension talks with the club until after their finals campaign and his clear mind helped Trent Robinson's men gain just their second win over Penrith in 14 meetings since the start of 2020.

The Tricolours produced a strong defensive performance in the highly-anticipated clash. (Getty Images: Matt King )

Cherry-Evans opened and finished the scoring and still looks every bit an NRL player as rumours swirl that the 37-year-old playmaker will head to the Super League for a career swansong next year.

The Roosters, who have won their last eight consecutive games, face Wests Tigers, the Dolphins and South Sydney to round out their regular season.

Penrith, meanwhile, could drop out of the top two by the end of the weekend after being the competition leaders since Round 4.

In their first hit-out since losing captain Isaah Yeo to a pectoral injury, Ivan Cleary's side lacked direction in attack and have now lost five of their past eight games.

The Panthers went desperately close to opening the scoring with a 14-pass move putting Brian To'o in the clear to touch down, only for the winger to step in to touch at the last minute.

The Roosters remained camped in their own half until a wayward Nathan Cleary pass fell to Mark Nawaqanitawase to relieve the pressure on Robinson's side.

In an instant, the Tricolours were up the other end and Cherry-Evans burst past a flat-footed Isaiah Papali'i to score in the 20th minute.

Walker converted and the Roosters should feel aggrieved for not doubling their lead as halftime approached when Rob Toia had a try chalked off.

Nawaqanitawase was penalised for a disruptor penalty that Canterbury football manager Phil Gould described in commentary for the Nine Network as "a disgraceful call and a disgraceful rule".

Walker kicked a penalty goal on halftime after a push and shove between Dylan Edwards and Connor Watson to make it 8-0 at the break, condemning Penrith to a scoreless first half for the second week running.

The Panthers were lacking spark, but with 15 minutes left Ivan Cleary threw Blaize Talagi on at five-eighth and they immediately reacted to the shake-up.

After pounding the Roosters' line, Lindsay Smith slipped an offload away to fellow forward Moses Leota who powered over with a 67th-minute try.

Cleary kicked the conversion to make it 8-6, but the Panthers were unable to come up with a late knockout blow as Cherry-Evans scampered over with a 77th-minute match winner.

AAP

World.title: Gardner breaks silence on affair with teammate, retains vice-captaincy
World.content:
Australia vice-captain Ash Gardner has apologised for the pain caused by her marriage breakdown and thanked Cricket Australia for backing her leadership.

Gardner's affair with Australian teammate Georgia Voll while married to ex-wife Monica Wright created headlines.

Wright publicly questioned the lack of action by CA in the wake of the affair, calling attention to "a clear power imbalance" when a senior member of staff has an affair with a junior.

Wright said Gardner should not be allowed to stay as vice-captain and questioned why CA had said nothing on the matter.

Gardner's marriage breakdown came as the result of an affair with teammate Georgia Voll (pictured). (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg, speaking on SEN on Thursday, said "additional policies" would be put in place in situations where perceived or real conflicts of interest existed, when relationships between players had been disclosed.

He confirmed CA had been made aware of the relationship between Gardner and Voll before it appeared in the press, but also backed Gardner to stay in her position.

"Ash is a highly regarded leader in our system. The CA board make leadership decisions and have oversight over all leadership decisions," Greenberg said.

"Ash is our vice-captain for a reason, because she's highly regarded, but what we will do is in situations where there are personal relationships is make sure there are additional guardrails, so the perception of conflict or conflict itself — talking about things like selection — are handled appropriately and respectfully."

Todd Greenberg (pictured) says Gardner remains a highly-valued leader within the Australian team. (AAP: James Ross)

"We've got policies in place but we will put additional ones in place given Ash is now vice-captain. If there are relationships that have been disclosed and they have been, then we will make sure that conflict — perceived or real — around selections are removed, so Ash is not involved in those things."

Greenberg said the relationship between Gardner and Voll was "new news" in the media.

"But for those that were in the team and leading the team, we've been well across this for a period of time," he said.

Gardner addressed her affair and the position of the hierarchy in a post on Instagram.

"While my separation from my wife is a personal matter, I understand my current relationship status needed to be addressed by Cricket Australia given my position as vice-captain," Gardner wrote.

"I am grateful that the CA Board has chosen to support my continued leadership. I look forward to playing a strong role as a leader and providing the best possible support for my teammates in the season to come.

"I am grateful for the time Monica and I shared and sorry for the pain this has caused. I wish her nothing but happiness and success in the future.

"I won't be making any further public comment on this matter at this time and ask that the privacy of those involved is respected."

Greenberg made the point "respect" for all concerned was paramount.

"It is a very personal matter for the player, and I think there's a level of respect that needs to go with that," he said.

"Cricket's got very strong respect-at-work policies, so we've got a policy that's been developed over time that can deal with these sorts of things."

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: A 'peanut' jibe, a Starc record and a brain explosion
World.content:
Steve Smith called a Bangladesh bowler a "peanut" for making an appeal, but he could probably have labelled a couple of his batting colleagues as such on a dire batting display for Australia.

Meanwhile, Mitch Starc collected another accolade with yet another top order wicket for the Aussies

As it happened: Bangladesh minnows humble Australia's giants on day one in Darwin

Here are the quick hits from day one of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Weatherald falls in front of hometown crowd

Weatherald was unable to impress in front of his home crowd. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Local boy Jake Weatherald began the first Test under significant pressure, having clung onto his opening spot after struggling through his debut series against England.

And there was significant support for the Northern Territorian in Darwin, with the crowd rising and falling as he attempted to get his innings going.

But once again, Weatherald was unable to find his feet at Test level, eventually reaching and swiping and nicking off for an unconvincing 23 off 37 deliveries.

It was Weatherald's 10th sub-50 score from his 11 Test innings, and one that only raised more questions about his viability as a Test match opener

Weatherald, the first Australian men's Test cricketer born and raised in the Northern Territory and now the first Territorian to play Test cricket in Darwin, with three more opportunities to secure a spot on the plane to South Africa in October.

2. Green's pre-lunch brain explosion

Bangladesh was overjoyed to claim Green's wicket with the final ball before lunch. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With Australia teetering at 3-61, the under-pressure Cam Green decided to take the game on.

Perhaps the Australian most in need of a score, the all-rounder began his innings with a pair of well-timed drives, before hooking Taskin Ahmed for a maximum over backward square leg.

However, Green's counterattack was short lived, with the big man playing one shot too many in the shadows of the first break.

With what turned out to be the final ball of the morning session, Green all but gave his wicket away, meekly chipping one to a grateful Mushfiqur Rahim on the on-side.

Australia headed to lunch at 4-74, Bangladesh couldn't believe their luck, and Green, having come out with such purpose, trudged off for a run-a-ball 13.

3. Smith's triple reprieve

So often the man for a crisis, Steve Smith is no stranger to standing tall as wickets tumble around him.

But Australia's idiosyncratic world beater was anything but convincing as he somehow managed to prod his way to lunch after coming to the crease at 2-52.

Smith should have been out on 2, with his thick edge falling through the fingers of a stooping second slip.

A matter of balls later, Smith was once again nicking towards the cordon — but this time, the ball flew through a gap between second slip and gully, with Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto having only just removed a man from behind the wicket.

And it appeared that Smith's luck was well and truly in when he survived a line-ball DRS review.

With Smith swinging hard outside off, Bangladesh went up for caught behind with some confidence. Umpire Kumar Dharmasena was unmoved, and Shanto wasted no time in sending the decision upstairs.

The technology, however, showed no conclusive evidence of an edge, with the ball passing perilously close to Smith's blade but failing to make its mark on ultra edge.

Bangladesh couldn't believe it as Smith was handed his third reprieve of the morning.

4. Smith talks Bangladesh out of a review, lands "peanut" jibe

Smith talked Bangladesh out of a review before late in the second session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having burnt two reviews in the first session, Bangladesh had just one DRS Hail Mary to play with for the bulk of the Australian innings.

Late in the second session, seamer Ebadot Hussein was tempted to break the glass for one that he never should have been.

His LBW shout against Smith was clearly far too high, but that didn't stop the Bangladeshi brains trust gathering for a serious discussion in the middle.

Smith couldn't believe it.

"Knee roll you reckon? It was up here you peanut!" Smith could be heard saying through the stump mic, gesturing to his hip area.

"What game are you watching?"

Smith's derision was enough to talk Bangladesh out of the review, but his honesty didn't end up counting for much — the Australian vice-captain eventually top-edging a short ball to be caught for 71.

5. Starc makes history

Australia's Mitchell Starc added another record to his list. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

The records keep coming for Australia's top-order destroyer, Mitchell Starc.

Fresh from being named his country's Test player of the year last Friday, the 36-year-old carved out another piece of history, becoming the most lethal left arm bowler in the history of the format.

Starc procured a leading edge from opener Shadman Islam to claim the 434th wicket of his Test career, with Nathan Lyon making amends for an earlier dropped chance.

Starc's milestone scalp took him past former Sri Lanka spinner Rangana Herath.

However, that was the only breakthrough of the day in what was a humbling start to the season for Australia.

World.title: Pallister downs McIntosh to claim 200m gold medal at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's freestyle star Lani Pallister has collected gold and silver medals in her arduous opening to the Pan Pacific championships in the United States.

Pallister triumphed in the women's 200m freestyle and then set a personal best when finishing behind American legend Katie Ledecky in the 1500m freestyle in Irvine, California on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Dolphins teammates Sam Short (men's 800m freestyle), Brittany Castelluzzo (women's 200m butterfly) and Ben Armbruster (men's 50m butterfly) also triumphed on the opening night of the Pan Pacs.

The Dolphins won four of 11 gold medals on offer, with Pallister's remarkable year continuing.

Sam Short claimed gold in the men's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Just weeks after winning four Commonwealth Games gold medals in Glasgow, Pallister pipped Canadian ace Summer McIntosh in the 200m final.

The Australian clocked one minute 53.67 seconds — just 0.02s outside her personal best in the event — with McIntosh second in 1:53.86.

About two hours later, Pallister then returned to the pool for the gruelling 1500m freestyle and set a her best time over the distance.

In what was essentially a match race against peerless American great Ledecky, who hasn't lost in the event in 16 years, Pallister put in a gallant effort.

Lani Pallister (left) and Moesha Johnson (right) were beaten out by Katie Ledecky (centre) in the 1500m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

The 26-year-old shadowed Ledecky, the winner of nine Olympic and 23 world championship gold medals, for the initial 500 metres.

The American great then produced her renowned burst to create a handy advantage en route to touching in 15:36.09.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pallister's 15:38.62 eclipsed her previous best of 15:39.14 from June last year.

In the men's 800m freestyle, Short went close to a personal best as he edged American rival Bobby Finke.

Short clocked 7:37.02, just 0.71s shy of his best time in the event, with Finke finishing some five-and-a-half seconds behind in second.

Earlier, Armbruster claimed Australia's first gold medal of the pool meet, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.75 seconds, 0.02s outside the Australian record jointly held by Kyle Chalmers and Matt Targett.

And Castelluzzo took out the women's 200m 'fly in 2:06.24 from her Dolphins teammate Liz Dekkers (2:06.56).

AAP

World.title: 'I'll remember the people': Sidebottom among retiring AFL premiership duo
World.content:
Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has officially told Magpies teammates he will be retiring at season's end.

The dual Magpies premiership hero's announcement on Thursday comes just hours after Richmond midfielder Dion Prestia also called it quits.

Debuting in 2009, Sidebottom has played 373 AFL games — the second most in Collingwood's storied history, only behind Scott Pendlebury.

A member of the Magpies' 2010 premiership side as a 19-year-old, Sidebottom then kicked a famous goal late in the 2023 grand final to help seal the club's next flag 13 years later.

Sidebottom (left) and Scott Pendlebury (right) have played the most matches together as teammates in VFL/AFL history. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

With Collingwood guaranteed to be in the wildcard round of the finals, at least, Sidebottom will be hoping for a fairytale farewell.

The versatile midfielder won Collingwood's Copeland Trophy in 2017 and 2018, also earning All-Australian honours once.

"As a young kid from 'Tally' [Tallygaroopna], I could never imagine I'd finish my AFL career with over 370 games, two premierships and 18 years of memories," Sidebottom said.

"When I look back on my time at Collingwood, I'll remember the people.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"So many teammates, coaches, staff and volunteers have invested their time and energy into helping me along the way."

Sidebottom might not be the only senior Collingwood player to retire this year, with Pendlebury also weighing up his future after breaking the VFL/AFL games record in May.

The Magpies have the oldest list in the AFL and are attempting to stay in premiership contention with a group in transition.

At Richmond, Prestia has joined premiership teammate Nathan Broad in ending his career.

After starting his career with Gold Coast, Prestia enjoyed instant success after making the switch to the Tigers in 2017.

Prestia won three premierships in his first four seasons with Richmond after joining at the end of 2016. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

The midfielder played in three premierships (2017, 2019, 2020) in his first four seasons at Richmond.

Despite being riddled by injury in 2020 and restricted to just five games during the pandemic season, Prestia returned to play an important role in all four of the Tigers' finals.

"I felt like a Richmond man from the very beginning," Prestia said.

"My decision to come to Richmond was not to prove what I could do, but to be a part of a club that I saw potential for greatness, and didn't we prove that right?"

Prestia and Broad will be given a farewell in front of the Richmond army this Saturday when the Tigers host St Kilda at the MCG.

AAP

World.title: Solomon rubbishes rumours of rifts with Essendon coaching candidates
World.content:
Interim Essendon coach Dean Solomon has described a rumoured falling-out with Mark McVeigh as like an "episode of Home and Away".

After Solomon chose not to put his hand up to be the Bombers' full-time coach, Essendon are closing in on announcing a leader as soon as next week.

McVeigh has been tipped to win the job, even ahead of Essendon icon James Hird.

It has led to suggestions of a rift among the trio, something Solomon has strenuously denied.

Solomon (centre) says there is no ill-feeling towards either Hird (left) or McVeigh (right) after pulling out of the Essendon coaching race. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"We don't know where they've come from — they're rumours," Solomon said.

"[McVeigh's has been] one of my best mates since the age of 15.

"I've known Hirdy since the age of 17.

"The talks with me potentially not being here next year, whether that stimulated a bit of that conversation, we're unsure.

"But I feel like it's a bit of an episode of [long-running Australian TV soapie] Home and Away.

McVeigh, currently an assistant with Sydney, has been touted as the favourte to win the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"There's nothing there. We all want to see this club heading in the right direction."

Solomon, McVeigh and Hird all played together at the Bombers, with Solomon and Hird playing in Essendon's most recent premiership side in 2000. McVeigh played with the pair in a losing grand final in 2001.

The trio also worked together briefly at GWS when McVeigh was the Giants' interim coach in 2022.

Solomon initially declared he would stay on at the Bombers next year, even if he wasn't senior coach.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But his family remains living in northern NSW, complicating matters for him.

"Part of the process of thinking about going in the process for the senior coaching role was sitting down with my family and talking about that," Solomon said.

"My wife and kids live in northern NSW.

"I've had 10 to 11 months away from them at the moment.

"Is that sustainable long-term? It's probably not."

Solomon stressed the next coach didn't need to be an Essendon person, referencing the legendary Kevin Sheedy, who grew up supporting the Bombers but whose playing career was at Richmond.

"He just needs to be the right person," Solomon said.

"A lot of people surrounding our football club are really frustrated.

"We want to be great, and we want to be great really quickly.

"This is a big job and it's an exciting challenge."

AAP

World.title: Hulking prop set to be 1,000th Wallaby as Kiss reshuffles deck
World.content:
The 1,000th Wallaby is poised to be capped in Townsville after hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis was named on the bench to face Japan.

Les Kiss, in his second game in charge, has also recalled fly half Carter Gordon at Declan Meredith's expense.

With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii injured, he has given Isaac Henry a starting debut at outside centre a week after he earned his first minutes in a tight Osaka defeat of Eddie Jones's side.

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto's Test return has also been secured, the Queensland Reds firebrand set to partner Lachlan Shaw — in his starting debut — in the second row, with Jeremy Williams on the bench and Josh Canham rested.

The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way' The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Kiss has also shaken up the back row, with Charlie Cale and Carlo Tizzano to partner skipper Harry Wilson, leaving Fraser McReight on the bench and Rob Valetini out of the 23.

Brandon Paenga-Amosa will get his chance under Kiss as replacement hooker while Filipo Daugunu has also been included on the bench as backline cover.

Angus Bell and Taniela Tupou also return to the starting side after stirring second-half cameos in Osaka, while the back three are unchanged and Tate McDermott and Ben Donaldson again provide play-making options on the bench.

It continues the theme of Kiss's tenure, with the new coach keen to assess his options before a long run of Tests ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

"The coaches have looked to find some balance in the selection after what was a physically taxing Test week in the heat in Japan," Kiss said.

"The whole group has worked hard this week and we know where we need to improve.

"This Saturday in Townsville gives us an opportunity to grow and strengthen our game on home soil in front of our supporters."

Gordon impressed at fly half against Ireland, before missing the next two Tests with a calf injury.

Meredith started in the past three Tests alongside Brumbies clubmate Ryan Lonergan, who has been retained the starting scrum half role.

WALLABIES (1-15): Angus Bell, Josh Nasser, Taniela Tupou, Lachlan Shaw, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Carlo Tizzano, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Carter Gordon, Harry Potter, Hunter Paisami, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright.

BENCH (16-23): Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Jeremy Williams, Fraser McReight, Tate McDermott, Ben Donaldson, Filipo Daugunu

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm (AEST).

AAP

World.title: Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt
World.content:
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.

Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.

However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.

White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.

"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.

It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.

WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul Chicago's DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham, but stormed off only to post "white privilege" on social media minutes later.

Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".

White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.

Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.

Sophie Cunningham (right) first went viral after becoming Caitlin Clark's unofficial bodyguard on the court for the Fever. (Getty Images: Jess Rapfogel)

The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.

A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.

For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.

Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

Sophie Cunningham has no problems being the villain on her Fever team. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".

"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.

"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.

Cheryl Reeve has shown her support to the transgender community in the wake of Sophie Cunningham's comments. (Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.

Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.

"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.

While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".

Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.

Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.

It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.

White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".

Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.

Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.

The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.

She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.

There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.

Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.

Republican party's bid to claim Clark

Caitlin Clark's arrival in the WNBA has seen the league's popularity skyrocket over the past two seasons. (Getty Images: Michael Hickey)

Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.

While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.

Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.

That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.

Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.

The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".

The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".

Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.

As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.

Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".

Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.

A bizarre sex toy invasion

The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.

Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.

The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.

Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.

Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.

One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.

"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens," she said.

Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".

"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.

"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."

Loading...

The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.

A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.

Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.

That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.

Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

Tech.title: 2K launches new studio to build its ‘next blockbuster sports franchise’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

2K is launching a new AAA game development studio, Small Axe Studios, with an ambitious goal: to build the company’s “next blockbuster sports franchise,” according to a LinkedIn post.

The post doesn’t explicitly say what sport this new game will focus on. But an image included in the post features what appears to be a mockup soccer badge, indicating that Small Axe might be making a soccer game that goes head-to-head with EA Sports FC. The Small Axe website also lists senior staffers with experience working on EA’s FIFA series (the former name of EA Sports FC), including studio head Aaron McHardy, who once led that franchise.

Small Axe was born from 2K Sports Lab, a project 2K announced in 2023. Whatever this new game is, it will add to 2K’s existing roster of games covering sports such as basketball (NBA 2K), wrestling (WWE 2K), and golf (PGA Tour 2K).

Tech.title: Ford’s $28,000 Fathom EV nears production after $2 billion factory overhaul
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ford said today that its next-generation electric vehicle — recently dubbed Fathom — will go into production at the automaker’s recently overhauled Louisville Assembly Plant in the first quarter of 2027.
